props.name: tests on 46 samples from production charges gave the thermograms and synthesis properties
props.note: only 14 charges are reported individually
props.statement: Thermograms and synthesis properties were determined in tests on 46 samples from production charges; 14 charges are shown in Abb. 1 and the table.

props.name: thermographic testing solved the activity-control problems in production; valid only for the same preparation recipe
props.scope: catalysts made by the same recipe
props.statement: Thermographic testing of the catalysts quickly and well solved all problems of activity control in the author's works and has proved itself in production control; the relations hold only when the same recipes are used for the preparation.

props.name: nitrate up to 0.03 wt% NO3 is harmless and gives no exothermic effect
props.note: the tests behind this statement are not described
props.statement: According to the author's tests, contents up to 0.03 wt% NO3 are harmless and also show no exothermic effect in the thermogram.

props.name: charges without an exothermic peak were very active; exothermic peaks indicate preparation faults and inactive catalysts
props.statement: The unequal thermal effects indicate differences between charges: the charges without an exothermic peak were very active, exothermic effects show that the preparation procedure was not followed, and exothermic effects in the thermogram are a sign of inactive catalysts.

props.name: quality control previously relied on synthesis in test reactors (slow, costly); methanol decomposition at normal pressure only approximately related (cited)
props.note: cited from refs. 1-5 (Cryder and Frolich; Dohse; Frolich; Hüttig and Kostelitz; Huffman and Dodge)
props.statement: Quality control of methanol catalysts previously relied almost exclusively on synthesis in test reactors, which is very time-consuming and costly; judging activity by catalytic methanol decomposition at normal pressure is more advantageous, but only an approximate relation between formation and decomposition has been found for some catalysts.

props.name: morphological, chemical, physical and mechanical checks of charges gave no basis for judging activity
props.statement: Each production charge is checked for morphological, chemical, physical and mechanical properties, but these investigations gave no suitable basis for judging the activity of the catalysts.

props.name: some thermograms show only endothermic peaks at 150 °C and about 220 °C; others also an exothermic peak at about 280 °C
props.statement: The thermograms of the production charges differ: some curves have only endothermic peaks at 150 °C and about 220 °C, others additionally an exothermic peak at about 280 °C.

props.name: earlier proposed mechanisms (cited): termolecular (Natta et al.), bimolecular via formaldehyde, methanol desorption, Knudsen diffusion
props.note: cited from refs. 1-6
props.statement: Mechanisms proposed earlier include a termolecular surface reaction of two adsorbed hydrogen molecules and adsorbed CO (Natta, Mazzanti and Pasquon), a bimolecular scheme via formaldehyde with either step rate-determining (Natta and Pastonesi; Ozaki and Saita; Pasquon), rate-determining desorption of methanol (Uchida and Ogino), and Knudsen diffusion of methanol in the pores (Cherednichenko and Temkin).

props.name: rate and equilibrium amounts of H2 and CO chemisorption are mutually enhanced by the other gas
props.statement: The rate as well as the equilibrium amounts of chemisorption of hydrogen and of carbon monoxide on the three-component methanol synthesis catalyst are mutually enhanced by the presence of the other gas; mixed adsorption exceeds separate adsorption.

props.name: earlier paper (cited): r = k P_H2 A_CO; adsorbed species CH3O not CH2O; Eley-Rideal reaction of H2 gas with adsorbed CH3O rate-determining

evidence.note: rendered: 'is CH3O and not CH2O'; quote withheld: sha256:2a6eb73f119c17d07c254cac8beae04caef47ce7c3d7950454d8c759c6a1c167 chars:80

props.note: cited from Tsuchiya and Shiba, Shokubai 4, 27 (1962); not this paper's measurement
props.statement: In the authors' earlier paper (ref. 10), by Tamaru's method, the methanol synthesis rate was r = k P_H2 A_CO (A_CO: CO adsorbed in any surface complex), or Uchida-Ogino's equation with α nearly 0.7; the adsorbed species had the stoichiometric formula CH3O, not CH2O; the reaction between hydrogen gas and adsorbed CH3O (Eley-Rideal type) was concluded to be rate-determining.

props.name: the mutual enhancement of adsorption has a certain saturation

evidence.quote: These results suggest that the mutual enhance- ment of adsorption has a certain saturation.

props.statement: The mutual enhancement of adsorption has a certain saturation (knick points in Fig. 4), suggesting some excess adsorption of either gas that does not form a complex, though small.

props.name: alternatively: creation of additional sites (Zn-H) by H2 chemisorption (Nagarjunan, Sastri and Kuriacose)
props.statement: The enhancement might be due to the creation of additional sites: hydrogen chemisorption creates additional donor levels, reduces the surface charge barrier and forms e.g. Zn-H bonds favourable for CO adsorption, while CO facilitates Zn-H formation.

props.name: mutual enhancement explained by surface-complex formation
props.statement: The mutual enhancement of H2 and CO adsorption is explained by the formation of a surface complex; on this typical three-component catalyst and at these temperatures complex formation is highly probable.

props.name: the surface complex (at least its major part) is the intermediate of methanol synthesis

props.statement: Since even the best catalysts cannot suppress the reaction temperature much below 300 °C, where equilibrium gives practically no methanol at atmospheric pressure, past attempts to synthesize methanol at atmospheric pressure were bound to fail; at 1000 lb/in2 equilibrium is still favorable to practically 100 per cent methanol at 300 °C.

props.name: conclusions: active at lower temperature, sensitive to poisons

evidence.quote: The catalyst in question, consisting of the oxides of copper, zinc, and alu- minum supported on metallic copper, appears to be most active at lower temperature and suffers a permanent de- crease in activity when exposed to higher temperatures.
Also the catalyst is sensitive to poisons.
By connecting several chambers in series, however, it is possible to dispose of the catalyst poison in the first chamber, thus protecting the contact material contained in subsequent reactors.

props.statement: The copper-zinc-aluminum oxide catalyst on metallic copper appears most active at lower temperature, suffers a permanent decrease in activity when exposed to higher temperatures, and is sensitive to poisons; connecting several chambers in series disposes of the poison in the first chamber and protects the contact material in subsequent reactors.

props.name: conclusions: high-purity methanol over metallic oxides

evidence.quote: Methanol of high purity may readily be prepared by passing a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, pref- erably at a pressure of several hundred atmospheres and at temperatures between 300° and 350° C., over a catalyst composed of metallic oxides.

Working with a catalyst of medium activity prepared from the oxides of copper, zinc, and aluminum, it is possible to reach nearly theoretical conversion depending upon the pressure, temperature, and rate of gas flow employed.
Carbon dioxide, water, and methane may form, but the amount of carbon monoxide consumed in these side reactions is small under the conditions most favorable to methanol formation.

props.statement: Methanol of high purity may readily be prepared by passing CO and H2, preferably at several hundred atmospheres and 300-350 °C, over a catalyst composed of metallic oxides; with the medium-activity copper-zinc-aluminum oxide catalyst nearly theoretical conversion can be reached depending on pressure, temperature and gas flow, and CO consumed in side reactions (CO2, water, methane) is small under the most favorable conditions.

props.name: percentage conversion decreases with flow

evidence.quote: While the quantity of methanol formed per unit time increases with the rate of gas flow, the percentage conversion of carbon mon- oxide decreases owing to the shorter time of contact be- tween the reacting gas and the catalyst.

props.statement: While the quantity of methanol formed per unit time increases with the rate of gas flow, the percentage conversion of carbon monoxide decreases owing to the shorter contact time.

props.name: activity decrease due to poisoning

evidence.quote: The results demonstrate that the decrease in activity is due to poisoning.
Figure 11 brings this out most clearly.

The conversion in the first chamber decreases from 25 per cent and reaches a constant value of about 8 per cent, while the second chamber, which is protected against poisoning by the first chamber, gives a constant yield of from 40 to 42 per cent for about 18 hours.

During the first 20 hours at an average temperature of 298° C., the yield drops from 32 to 12 per cent, showing that the activity of the catalyst decreases with the time when only a single chamber is used.

props.statement: With unpurified gas, catalyst activity decreases with time in a single chamber; the two-chamber runs demonstrate that the decrease is due to poisoning: chamber 1 falls from 25 to about 8 per cent while the protected chamber 2 gives a constant 40-42 per cent for about 18 hours.

props.name: equilibrium calculations only qualitative

props.statement: Without identifying the poison, the series experiments show that the first chamber in a series acts as a purifier for the gas mixture, removing substances that act as catalyst poisons and protecting the catalyst in successive chambers.

props.name: iron-alkali: side reactions hard to suppress

evidence.quote: In general, the results obtained with this type of catalyst show that it is very difficult to suppress side reactions leading to the formation of carbon dioxide, methane, water, and elementary carbon.

props.statement: With iron-alkali catalysts it is very difficult to suppress side reactions leading to carbon dioxide, methane, water and elementary carbon; the liquid separates into a watery layer and an oily layer of simpler oxygenated aliphatic compounds and hydrocarbons; for both catalyst types the CO lost in side reactions is serious, the iron-alkali catalysts being inferior to the oxide mixtures in this respect.

props.name: best oxide result: runs 278A and B

evidence.quote: The total yield of alcohols from these runs based on the entering carbon monoxide was 13.9 per cent, and the waste amounted to 34.1 per cent.

Normal propanol was the most important organic constituent, with a yield of 4.5 per cent.
These were the best results obtained in any of the experiments reported in Table V.

props.statement: Runs 278A and B (I-47-1) gave the best results of Table V: total alcohols 13.9 per cent of entering CO, waste 34.1 per cent, alcohols other than methanol 11.3 per cent, normal propanol the most important organic constituent at 4.5 per cent.

props.name: high-chromium alloys unsatisfactory

evidence.quote: As a whole the results were decidedly unsatisfac- tory.
Either no reaction or only very slight activity was observed in every case ex- cept with catalyst II—30—1 (2.75 per cent chromium steel).

props.statement: The catalysts of Table I (chromium and iron alloys and metals with potassium oxide) gave decidedly unsatisfactory results: no reaction or only very slight activity, except catalyst II-30-1 (2.75 per cent chromium steel).

props.name: critical temperature for oily layer

evidence.quote: From these observations it is apparent that a critical temperature exists below which the formation of an oily layer is not observed.
Before this temperature is reached some higher alcohols may be formed and dissolved in the aqueous layer.

props.statement: A critical temperature exists below which no oily layer forms (468 °C for I-48-1 on repetition, 470 °C for I-47-1 in runs 278A and B, 450-490 °C for I-70-1); before it is reached some higher alcohols may form and dissolve in the aqueous layer.

props.name: Fischer's results reproduced with KOH-impregnated iron

evidence.quote: Preliminary experiments demonstrated that it was possible to reproduce Fischer’s results using as the catalyst iron or steel turnings impregnated with potassium hydroxide.
Char- acteristic of this process is the formation of a liquid product consisting of an aqueous and an oily layer.

props.statement: Preliminary experiments reproduced Fischer's results with iron or steel turnings impregnated with potassium hydroxide, giving a liquid product of an aqueous and an oily layer.

props.name: iron-alkali: more oil, disproportionately more waste

evidence.quote: On the basis of entering carbon monoxide, 13.9 per cent of useful products were obtained with the oxide catalyst, 10.5 per cent appearing in the oily layer and 3.4 per cent in the aqueous layer.
Of the 16.8 per cent of useful products obtained with the iron-alkali catalyst, 13.4 per cent appeared in the oily layer, and 3.4 per cent in the aqueous layer.
ucts in the oily layer, the waste products formed by the reaction are disproportionately higher than with the oxide catalyst.

props.statement: Comparing the best results (Table VII): the oxide catalyst gave 13.9 per cent useful products (10.5 oily, 3.4 aqueous; 11.3 other than methanol), the iron-alkali catalyst 16.8 per cent (13.4 oily, 3.4 aqueous); the iron-alkali catalyst gives a slightly larger oily yield but disproportionately more waste products (56.7 against 34.1 per cent).

props.name: losses considerable; high temperature responsible

evidence.quote: From a study of these data it is apparent that the portion of carbon monoxide lost in wasteful side reactions is con- siderable for both iron-alkali and metallic oxide catalysts.
there can be no doubt that the high temperature of operation is respon- sible for a large part of the losses.
that the higher the temperature the greater the tendency for wasteful side reactions to occur.

props.statement: The portion of CO lost in wasteful side reactions is considerable for both iron-alkali and metallic oxide catalysts; some CO2 formation may be unavoidable, but the high operating temperature is responsible for a large part of the losses: the higher the temperature, the greater the tendency for wasteful side reactions.

props.name: lower chromium content reduces gaseous products

evidence.quote: The reduction of the chromium content of the steel from 12-14 per cent to 2.75 per cent, with an accompanying in- crease in the carbon content from 0.35 per cent to 0.9 per cent,
has not materially changed the yield of aqueous and oily products, but it has decreased the yield of gaseous products from 56.7 per cent to 38.5 per cent.

props.statement: Reducing the chromium content of the steel from 12-14 to 2.75 per cent (with carbon content rising from 0.35 to 0.9 per cent) did not materially change the aqueous and oily yields but decreased the gaseous products from 56.7 to 38.5 per cent.

props.name: low-chromium steel offers best possibilities

evidence.quote: In view of these data and the negative results with alloys of high chromium content (Table I), it seems that a low- chromium steel offers the best possibilities of efficient oil formation.

props.statement: In view of these data and the negative results with high-chromium alloys, a low-chromium steel seems to offer the best possibilities of efficient oil formation.

props.name: smallest KOH content gives best yields

evidence.quote: The best yields were obtained with the catalyst (11-25- 1) containing the smallest amount of potassium hydroxide (2.2 per cent potassium oxide).

There is apparently little difference in the aqueous and oily yield with 4.5 per cent and 8.5 per cent potassium oxide, but a considerable change, from 31.6 per cent to 79.4 per cent, is observed in the conver- sion of carbon monoxide to gaseous products.

props.statement: Of the chromium-steel catalysts with 2.2, 4.5 and 8.5 per cent potassium oxide, the best yields were obtained with II-25-1 (2.2 per cent); 4.5 and 8.5 per cent differ little in aqueous and oily yield, but CO to gaseous products changes from 31.6 to 79.4 per cent.

props.name: lower flow gives more oil and more gaseous loss

evidence.quote: It was noticed that the lower rate of flow produced more oil than the higher, although the actual amounts were small.

props.statement: With the methanol catalyst followed by the iron-alkali catalyst at 325 °C, the lower flow produced more oil than the higher (small amounts); this corresponds to a higher percentage of CO converted to gaseous products, while CO to total liquid is about the same; higher alcohols were detected but not identified.

props.name: methanol catalyst first gives smaller losses

props.name: oil production accompanied by CO loss

props.name: oxide catalysts most promising

evidence.quote: From the point of view of losses, the metallic oxide catalysts seem most promising in that they do not possess the marked tend-
ency to form methane, as do the contact substances con- taining metals of the iron group.
Furthermore, the useful products from the oxide catalysts consist mainly, if not wholly, of alcohols, while the iron-alkali catalysts are more uncon- trolled in their action

props.statement: From the point of view of losses the metallic oxide catalysts seem most promising: they lack the marked tendency to form methane of contact substances containing iron-group metals, and their useful products are mainly, if not wholly, alcohols, whereas the iron-alkali catalysts are more uncontrolled, giving complex mixtures of simpler oxygenated aliphatic compounds and straight paraffins.

props.name: oxide catalysts need 450-500 °C for higher alcohols

evidence.quote: Extensive preliminary experiments demonstrated that temperature entered as a most important variable when catalysts composed of metallic oxides were employed.
Thus, higher alcohols did not form unless temperatures around 450° to 500° C. were reached, which is considerably higher than the 300° to 350° C. required for methanol formation.

props.note: the preliminary experiments are not reported individually
props.statement: With metallic oxide catalysts temperature is a most important variable: higher alcohols did not form unless about 450 to 500 °C was reached, considerably higher than the 300 to 350 °C required for methanol formation.

props.name: product types differ above 80 °C

evidence.quote: Although the two give about the same amount boiling below 80° C., a marked diver- gence occurs above this point.
The exact nature of the substances obtained with the iron-alkali catalysts has not been determined.

props.statement: The two catalyst types give about the same amount of product boiling below 80 °C but diverge markedly above; the oxide-catalyst products consist mainly of higher alcohols, while the exact nature of the iron-alkali products was not determined (considered, in view of Fischer's results, a mixture of higher alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, acids and some higher hydrocarbons).

props.name: run 168B a novel result

evidence.quote: From this it would seem that a novel result was obtained in run 168B (Table IV), in which a compara- tively large ratio of oil to aqueous products was obtained at 334° C. using a 12 per cent chromium steel-alkali catalyst.

props.note: the comparison is with Fischer's conditions (cited)
props.statement: Compared with Fischer's best results at 410 °C, run 168B, giving a comparatively large ratio of oil to aqueous products at 334 °C with a 12 per cent chromium steel-alkali catalyst, seems a novel result; this prompted a study of the chromium content.

props.name: long runs 182 and 183 differ in efficiency

evidence.quote: As shown in section 6 of Table IV, considerable difference was found between the efficiencies of conversion in the two runs.
The product from run 182 contained about 75 per cent methanol, while 183 was lower in methanol (45 per cent) but contained a larger quantity of higher alcohols.
Fractionations disclosed higher alcohols while methanol was present in predominating quantities.

props.note: The source does not attribute the difference to the reduction period explicitly.
props.statement: The two 24-hour runs 182 and 183 (differing in the reduction period, 1 3/4 vs 3 1/2 h) showed considerable difference in conversion efficiencies; only a few drops of oil appeared; methanol predominated, run 182 giving about 75 per cent methanol and run 183 45 per cent with more higher alcohols.

props.name: temperature more important than pressure and flow

evidence.quote: In general, the pressure and gas flow were kept within the range recommended in the various patents and seem to be far less important than the temperatures which define so sharply the region between methanol formation and higher alcohol formation.

props.name: local overheating or cold top layers in the catalyst

props.name: activity maximum 60 70 zno

evidence.quote: With increasing percentages of zinc oxide the activity of the catalysts for methanol synthesis increases, at first slowly, then in the neighborhood of the 50 mol per cent point very rapidly, reaching a maximum between 60 and 70 mol per cent, and finally falling off somewhat toward the point cor- responding to pure zinc oxide.

props.statement: With increasing zinc oxide the methanol-synthesis activity increases, at first slowly, then very rapidly near 50 mol per cent, reaching a maximum between 60 and 70 mol per cent ZnO, and finally falls off somewhat toward pure zinc oxide.

props.name: bath temperature offset

evidence.quote: Since the methanol reaction is quite exothermic, the tem- perature of the bath may be somewhat lower than that of the catalyst, but not more than 10° C. lower
this does not seriously affect the relation between catalyst composition and activity.

props.statement: Because the methanol reaction is quite exothermic the bath temperature may be somewhat lower than that of the catalyst, but not more than 10 °C lower; this does not seriously affect the relation between catalyst composition and activity.

props.name: contact time effect negligible

evidence.quote: Thus, the rate of entering gas flow varied with the methanol production so as to give a somewhat shorter time of contact for the more active catalysts.
but the effect can be neglected for any practical purpose.

props.statement: Operating at constant exit-gas flow gives a somewhat shorter contact time for the more active catalysts, which tends to reduce their percentage conversion, but the effect can be neglected for any practical purpose.

props.name: copper rich mixtures poor

evidence.quote: From the curves in Figure 2 it is apparent that the mixtures consisting essentially of copper are exceedingly poor catalysts for the synthesis of methanol.

props.statement: Mixtures consisting essentially of copper are exceedingly poor catalysts for the synthesis of methanol.

props.name: decomposition method fit for testing

evidence.quote: In the absence of similar data on other catalyst mixtures it seems justifiable to conclude that the decomposition method of testing is eminently fitted for studies of the activity of catalysts

props.limitations: in the absence of similar data on other catalyst mixtures
props.statement: The decomposition method of testing is eminently fitted for studies of the activity of catalysts for methanol synthesis from water gas at high pressure.

props.name: decomposition method simpler and illuminating

evidence.quote: the decomposition at atmos- pheric pressure is a much simpler method of catalyst-testing than the direct synthesis of the alcohol at high pressure
The decomposition method of catalyst study therefore promises to be a valuable tool in researches on the synthesis of higher alcohols and more complicated organic compounds.

props.statement: Decomposition at atmospheric pressure is a much simpler method of catalyst testing than direct synthesis at high pressure and is greatly illuminating for disclosing the mechanism of the underlying reactions; it therefore promises to be a valuable tool in research on the synthesis of higher alcohols and more complicated organic compounds.

props.name: no methyl formate in synthesis

evidence.quote: formation of methyl formate, by polymerization of the supposedly intermediately formed formaldehyde, does
not occur in the high-pressure synthesis of methanol with these catalysts.

props.note: 'supposedly intermediately formed formaldehyde' refers to the decomposition scheme of the first paper
props.statement: Formation of methyl formate does not occur in the high-pressure synthesis of methanol with these catalysts.

props.name: slight activity loss over cycle

evidence.quote: From the two curves for 320° C. in Figure 2 it follows that there is a slight but measurable decrease in activity of these copper-zinc oxide catalysts during the cycle

props.statement: There is a slight but measurable decrease in activity of the copper-zinc oxide catalysts during the cycle of about 8 hours between 320 and 370 °C.

props.name: synthesis matches decomposition

evidence.quote: The resemblance of the synthesis curves to the carbon monoxide curves obtained
It is apparent that, within the experimental error, the two curves coincide in the neigh- borhood of the 50 mol per cent point, where the break occurs.
Except for this upper region, the two curves show no divergency in their general shape.

props.limitations: the decomposition curve is somewhat uncertain for the pure zinc oxide catalysts
props.note: the decomposition data are cited from the first paper of the series (reference 2); only the synthesis data are this paper's
props.statement: The synthesis activity curve resembles the carbon monoxide curve of the methanol decomposition work: within the experimental error the two curves coincide near the 50 mol per cent point where the break occurs, and show no divergency in general shape except for 97 to 100 mol per cent zinc, where the decomposition values are uncertain.

props.name: synthesis remote from equilibrium

evidence.quote: it seems safe to con- clude that the synthesis curves also represent conditions re- mote from equilibrium
it follows, therefore, that the decomposition data were obtained sufficiently far from equilibrium to make the results representative of the activity of the catalysts used.

props.note: the comparison is made with equilibrium data previously published by the same laboratory (reference 4, cited)
props.statement: The synthesis curves represent conditions remote from equilibrium (and the decomposition data were obtained sufficiently far from equilibrium to represent catalyst activity), although the equilibrium data for high-pressure methanol synthesis are somewhat unreliable.

props.name: high-pressure catalyst-testing reactor (Figure 1)
props.description: Outer steel tube with steel cap and brass lining; thin-walled brass catalyst tube; the inlet gas passes down the annular space and is preheated before reaching the catalyst held in the lower end of the brass tube on a copper screen spiral (catalyst in a roll of fine copper gauze). Submerged in a lead (lead-antimony) bath whose temperature is measured by a pyrometer; no pyrometer well in the catalyst. A small hole fitted with pipe F leads to a water trap to detect leakage through the lining.

evidence.quote: The reactor consists of an outer steel tube, A, fitted with a steel cap, B, at one end. Inside this tube fits a brass lining, C, turned from a solid rod to avoid the difficulty of sealing one end.
The catalyst chamber is a thin-walled brass tube which fits rather loosely into the brass lining.
The catalyst is ground to 60 mesh and supported on a copper screen spiral, 3-cc. samples of the powdered catalyst mixture being used for each experiment.
For these reasons the reactor was submerged in a lead bath and the temperature of the bath measured by means of a pyrometer.
Figure 1—Reactor Used for Catalyst-Testing at High Pressure
It was therefore necessary to line all steel surfaces with some other metal, brass and copper being pref- erable.

props.name: copper-zinc oxide catalysts (complete series of compositions)
props.description: The binary copper-zinc oxide catalyst mixtures previously used in the authors' methanol decomposition and synthesis experiments, examined here by x-rays after use. Individual compositions are shown only on the abscissa of Figure 1 (mol per cent), which is not read here.

evidence.quote: The study of the complete series of copper-zinc oxide mix- tures demonstrates that at every composition the catalyst is decidedly crystalline, possessing the characteristic crystal structure of the two components.
It is interesting to compare these results with the activity measurements previously made with the same catalysts.

props.name: breaks in activity curves match lattice discontinuities

evidence.quote: It is particularly interesting to note that a break in the activity curves invariably corre- sponds to a point of discontinuity in the lattice dimensions.
the only difference being that the atomic disarrangement occurs within a somewhat wider range of catalyst composition than does the change in preferential catalytic activity.

props.statement: A break in the activity curves invariably corresponds to a point of discontinuity in the lattice dimensions, even for the small zinc oxide percentages that cause the methyl formate peak; the atomic disarrangement occurs within a somewhat wider composition range than the change in preferential catalytic activity.

props.name: catalysis associated with internal crystal structure

evidence.quote: The foregoing re- sults point to an im- portant relation be- tween selective cata- lytic activity and distance between the atoms in mixed cata- lysts.

It is particu- larly noteworthy that catalysis, which apparently is a sur- face effect, seems to be closely associated with the internal structure of the crys- talline catalytic material as disclosed by x-ray analysis.

props.statement: The results point to an important relation between selective catalytic activity and interatomic distance in mixed catalysts; catalysis, apparently a surface effect, seems closely associated with the internal structure of the crystalline catalytic material as disclosed by x-ray analysis.

props.name: copper lattice expands with zinc oxide

evidence.quote: However, the unit-cell sizes of both are markedly influenced by the presence of the other constituent.

the side of the unit cell of the copper lattice expands with increasing additions of zinc oxide, passes through a maximum between 50 and 60 mol per cent zinc oxide, decreases somewhat, and then rises again.
The maxi- mum elongation recorded is 1.3 per cent, corresponding to 90 mol per cent zinc oxide, which is the highest concentration studied.

props.statement: The unit cell of the copper lattice expands with increasing zinc oxide, passes through a maximum between 50 and 60 mol per cent zinc oxide, decreases somewhat and rises again; the maximum elongation recorded is 1.3 per cent at 90 mol per cent zinc oxide, the highest concentration studied.

props.name: catalysts decidedly crystalline at every composition

evidence.quote: The study of the complete series of copper-zinc oxide mix- tures demonstrates that at every composition the catalyst is decidedly crystalline, possessing the characteristic crystal structure of the two components.
The copper has the same structure as that of the metal in bulk, and the zinc oxide has the same structure as when prepared by any other method.
Over the whole range the structure of the catalyst mixtures is decidedly crystalline.

props.statement: At every composition the copper-zinc oxide catalyst is decidedly crystalline, possessing the characteristic crystal structures of the two components: copper with the structure of the bulk metal and zinc oxide with its usual structure.

props.name: essential feature is selectivity of decomposition mechanism

evidence.quote: it was pointed out in the first paper of this series2 that the percentage methanol decomposed varied only slightly after a small percentage of zinc oxide had been added to the relatively inactive pure copper.
Thus, the es- sential feature of these catalysts is their selec- tive nature with respect to the mechanism by which the decomposi- tion occurs.

props.note: based on the decomposition results of the first paper of the series (reference 2), cited
props.statement: Since the percentage of methanol decomposed varied only slightly once a small percentage of zinc oxide had been added to pure copper, the essential feature of these catalysts is their selective nature with respect to the mechanism of decomposition.

props.name: no final conclusions without data on other catalysts

evidence.quote: it is not justifiable to draw any final conclusions or make generalizations in the absence of data on other catalysts.

props.statement: While a simple relation may exist between selective catalytic activity and interatomic distance, it is not justifiable to draw final conclusions or generalize in the absence of data on other catalysts.

props.name: formaldehyde/methyl formate at copper end, CO with zinc oxide

evidence.quote: formaldehyde and particu- larly methyl formate pro- duction is characteristic of the copper end of the dia- gram, while carbon mon- oxide formation is closely associated with the zinc oxide.

props.note: drawn from the cited decomposition data of Figure 2
props.statement: From the decomposition data, formaldehyde and particularly methyl formate production is characteristic of the copper end of the diagram, while carbon monoxide formation is closely associated with the zinc oxide.

props.name: pure zinc oxide changed by methanol-vapor treatment

evidence.quote: even in the absence of copper the zinc oxide suffers some change during the treatment with methanol vapor at 200- 220° C., as evidenced by the fact that the pure zinc oxide thus treated has a=somewhat smaller unit cell than usually, 5.213 A. vs. 5.226 A.

props.statement: Even in the absence of copper, zinc oxide suffers some change during treatment with methanol vapor at 200-220 °C: the treated pure zinc oxide has a somewhat smaller unit cell than usual, 5.213 A. vs. 5.226 A.

props.name: whether reduction goes to elementary zinc undecided

evidence.quote: It is not possible to de- cide, however, whether this reduction proceeds down to elementary zinc, although the indications are that this is the case.

props.statement: It is not possible to decide whether the reduction of zinc oxide proceeds down to elementary zinc, although the indications are that this is the case.

props.name: selective catalytic activity related to atomic spacing

evidence.quote: The similarity in the shape of the curves in Figures 3 and 4 cannot be coincidental.
The general character of the two diagrams is convincing evidence of a relation between the selective catalytic activity and the atomic spacing of the copper-zinc oxide mixtures.
The results point to a definite relation between the specific catalytic effect and the distance between the atoms of the two components,
Figure 3—Expansion of Copper Lattice Compared with Methyl Formate Produc- tion (dotted line), Both as Function of Catalyst Composition
Figure 4—Change in Zinc Oxide Lattice Compared with Carbon Monoxide Forma- tion (dotted line), Both as Function of Catalyst Composition

props.statement: The similarity in shape of the lattice-dimension curves and the methyl formate and carbon monoxide curves (Figures 3 and 4) cannot be coincidental and is convincing evidence of a relation between the selective catalytic activity and the atomic spacing of the copper-zinc oxide mixtures.

props.name: weight loss not absolutely quantitative

evidence.quote: the results thus obtained are not absolutely quantitative since there is always a possibility of the oxide mixtures not being com- pletely dehydrated when the reduction is started.
Further- more, the loss in weight does not tell whether the zinc is reduced to the free metal or merely to a lower stage of oxi- dation.

props.statement: The loss in weight on reduction is not absolutely quantitative, because the oxide mixtures may not have been completely dehydrated when the reduction started, and it does not tell whether the zinc is reduced to the free metal or to a lower stage of oxidation.

props.name: zinc oxide lattice elongates with copper

evidence.quote: The unit cell of the zinc oxide suffers a similar elongation on addition of copper, with the exception that the curve first passes through a minimum value for 10 to 20 mol per cent copper.

The dimensions of the zinc oxide lattice have been determined along both the vertical and horizontal axes, but since the axial ratio remains practically constant it is apparent that the two curves have the same general form

props.statement: The unit cell of zinc oxide suffers a similar elongation on addition of copper, except that the curve first passes through a minimum at 10 to 20 mol per cent copper; the axial ratio remains practically constant.

props.name: zinc oxide partly reduced in presence of copper oxide

evidence.quote: Although zinc oxide is usually considered non-reducible at this temperature, it was, nevertheless, found to be partly reduced by the above treatment when present in mixture with copper oxide.
The reduction manifested itself in the present cata- lyst mixtures by a somewhat greater loss in weight than that corresponding to reduction of the copper oxide alone.
Zinc oxide, ordinarily considered a non- reducible compound, is undoubtedly partly reduced in the presence of copper oxide.

props.limitations: the loss-in-weight results are not absolutely quantitative, since the oxide mixtures may not have been completely dehydrated when reduction started
props.statement: Zinc oxide, ordinarily considered non-reducible, is partly reduced by the methanol-vapor treatment at about 200-220 °C when present in mixture with copper oxide, as shown by a greater loss in weight than corresponds to reduction of the copper oxide alone.

props.name: most known methanol catalysts give CO2 or water with methanol

props.name: chromium above 25 improves in use
props.statement: Catalysts containing less than 25 atomic per cent chromium suffered a decrease in activity during use, while those containing more than 25 atomic per cent chromium improved.

props.name: chromium prevents overheating loss
props.statement: Chromium markedly prevents the loss of activity suffered by catalysts of high zinc content when exposed to temperatures somewhat above the optimum operating temperature; catalysts with a Zn:Cr molecular ratio of about 1 showed continuous improvement during extended use above the temperature of maximum activity.

props.name: cr2o3 more active than zno
props.statement: Chromium oxide has more activity than zinc oxide (both precipitated by ammonia) when allowance is made for the shrinkage of the chromium oxide: 6.8 per cent at 56,000 space velocity adjusts to an estimated 9.3 per cent at 25,000, against 6.0 per cent for zinc oxide at 25,000; chromium oxide also gave purer methanol and was superior as regards injury at high temperature and breakage.

props.name: glow only 92 cr
props.statement: Only the 92 atomic per cent chromium catalyst displayed the glow phenomenon (spontaneous temperature rises) during the synthesis tests; higher temperatures in the preliminary treatment delayed the heat effect; all three samples lost 60 per cent of volume and 45 per cent of weight.

props.name: na2co3 zno more active
props.statement: Zinc oxide precipitated by sodium carbonate is markedly more active than zinc oxide precipitated by ammonium hydroxide; the most active zinc oxide was made with a slight insufficiency of sodium carbonate.

props.name: preliminary reduction low pressure
props.statement: In large-scale operation the shrinkage would be dealt with by carrying out the preliminary reduction in simple low-pressure equipment and transferring the catalyst to the high-pressure equipment with precautions against contamination or oxidation.

props.name: product nearly pure methanol
props.statement: The liquid product was substantially pure methanol with a small percentage of water; maximum methanol contents were 96.4 to 99.8 per cent by volume except for pure zinc oxide (86) and the 92 atomic per cent chromium catalyst (79); in all cases the methanol percentage decreased with increasing operating temperature.

props.name: reactor heat capacity kept glow low
props.statement: The relatively great heat capacity of the reactor kept the maximum glow temperatures low; the effect is an indication of the frequently observed glow phenomenon.

props.name: reproducibility
props.statement: Interrupted constant-temperature runs agreed within 2 per cent; a repeat of the whole preparation and testing of pure zinc oxide differed by less than 5 per cent; the total error in conversions was probably less than 10 per cent in all cases and less than 5 per cent at higher conversions.

props.name: shrinkage increases with chromium
props.statement: Catalysts charged unreduced shrank during testing, the shrinkage increasing with chromium content, so that results late in the tests of high-chromium catalysts were at actual space velocities more than double the recorded 25,000.

props.name: table3 applies to other compositions
props.statement: The agreement of the space-velocity-adjusted Table I results with Table II indicates that the Table III space velocity vs. conversion data can be safely applied to other catalysts of the same type but of quite different composition.

props.name: trivalent chromium superior
props.statement: Catalysts prepared by methods using chromic acid (chromium trioxide) as the chromium source are much less active than those made by ammonia precipitation from the nitrates, with the chromium initially trivalent.

props.name: wall thermocouple error
props.statement: The difference between a thermocouple on the outside wall and one at the center of the catalyst was an approximately linear function of the rate of heat evolution and practically independent of temperature: about 20 °C higher outside without reaction and about 20 °C lower at 16 per cent conversion; temperature measurements outside the pressure wall are therefore uncertain.

props.name: effect of pressure on the heat of the methanol reaction (Berthelot equation; Equation 19, Figure 1)

evidence.note: Equation 19 as printed: ΔHT,P = ΔHT,P° - 0.5411 P - (3255000/T²) P; quote withheld: sha256:ab1b0910e762360c8032aee6d9d43aeee869272732f57f08f54a0e1c02915c36 chars:100

props.method: Thermodynamic equation of state (∂H/∂P)T = V - T(∂V/∂T)P summed over the components with the Berthelot equation of state and the critical constants; ΔHT,P° at 1 atm from Equation 9 at each temperature.

figure_1.text_value: ΔHT,P plotted against pressure (100-400 atm) for 25-900 °C

props.verdict: Figure 1 shows clearly a range of stable optimum working conditions.

props.name: 250 atm heat independent of temperature
props.statement: At about 250 atm the heat of reaction is virtually independent of temperature; fluctuations around a working temperature of 300 °C would produce little effect on the heat of reaction, so a process operated in this region may be more easily controlled.

props.name: agree with practical values
props.scope: comparison with values quoted in Dodge (ref. 2); the quoted values are not given
props.statement: The calculated values agree with values quoted (ref. 2) under practical conditions.

props.name: conversion increases with pressure
props.statement: Conversion increases rapidly with pressure: Kp' increases rapidly with pressure, and the effect is enhanced by the fact that Kγ' becomes smaller with increasing pressure.

props.name: equilibrium state pressure dependent
props.statement: Although the equilibrium constant Ka is a function of temperature only, the equilibrium state of the system is strongly dependent on pressure.

props.name: equilibrium unfavorable at high temperature
props.statement: Because the reaction is exothermic, the equilibrium becomes more unfavorable for methanol as the temperature increases.

props.name: ideal gas heat independent of pressure
props.statement: If ideal conditions apply, pressure will not affect the heat of reaction; at elevated pressures the conditions are not ideal and pressure will affect the heat of reaction.

props.name: keep temperature low
props.statement: The heat of the methanol reaction increases with pressure, and because the reaction is exothermic, by the Le Chatelier-Braun effect the temperature should be kept as low as is practical for a maximum yield of methanol.

props.name: thermodynamics predicts optimum
props.statement: The thermodynamic study should be useful for predicting optimum values of temperature and pressure for new processes and for checking operating conditions of existing processes.

props.name: hot spots in large converters may cause methanization
props.statement: In large converters with integral heat exchange systems, hot spots may develop in the catalyst mass and become hot enough (about 400 °C) to produce methanization, which may cause both product losses and enforce shutdown by converter runaway.

props.name: van der Waals treatment would give the Berthelot result
props.note: the derivation is in ref. (11), printed '(77)' in the text layer
props.statement: A general thermodynamic equation derived with van der Waals' equation, not used for the methanol calculations, should lead to the same result as the Berthelot equation.

props.name: highest conversion with 8–28% Cu
props.statement: The highest conversion of CO2 to methanol was obtained with catalysts containing 8–28% Cu + 92–72% Al2O3, giving 94% at 410 atm and a catalyst temperature of 285°.

props.name: CO + H2 gives only 39–43% methanol with methane and dimethyl ether
props.statement: With carbon monoxide and hydrogen over copper-alumina catalysts (expts. 14–16), under conditions similar to those with CO2, methanol conversion was only 39–43%, while 10–15% and 32–41% of the CO charged gave methane and dimethyl ether.

props.name: adding CO2 almost eliminates ether and raises methanol
props.statement: Replacing only 25% of the carbon monoxide with carbon dioxide (expts. 17, 18) almost completely eliminated ether formation; at CO:CO2 = 3.1:1.0 methanol conversion rose to 64% and dimethyl ether fell to about 1%.

props.name: copper and alumina separately inactive; the mixture is necessary
props.statement: Copper and alumina, separately, did not catalyze methanol formation from carbon dioxide and hydrogen; the mixture of the two is necessary.

props.name: lower pressure reduces conversion; reaction stops at CO
props.statement: Lowering the pressure (expts. 10–12) from 409 to 117 atm reduced conversion from 94 to about 13%, the reaction at the lower pressures tending to stop with the reduction of the dioxide to the monoxide.

props.name: H2:CO2 ratio does not change the product type; methanol falls with less hydrogen
props.statement: Changing the hydrogen:carbon dioxide ratio (expts. 7–9) did not materially influence the type of products; the methanol yield fell off due to the decrease in the limiting reactant, hydrogen.

props.name: heat released in CO reduction causes methanol dehydration to ether
props.statement: In the CO experiments (expts. 14–16) the energy released caused catalyst temperatures about 30° above the furnace, and this energy caused dehydration of nascent methanol to dimethyl ether; no comparable release occurs with CO2 because the reduction of CO2 to CO is endothermic.

props.name: higher temperature lowers methanol conversion and raises methane and CO
props.statement: With the 62% Cu catalyst, increasing temperature (expts. 3–6) lowered the conversion to methanol from 85 to about 2% and increased conversion to methane and carbon monoxide from about 1% to 44 and 14%, respectively.

props.name: water experiments inconclusive
props.statement: Experiments with water (not tabulated) were inconclusive: ether formation was eliminated, but methanol conversion fell to about 4% and 62% of the CO charged reacted with water to form CO2.

props.name: CO2 → CO → formaldehyde → methanol via Cannizzaro on amphoteric alumina

evidence.quote: from carbon dioxide and hydrogen.
2HCHO + H20 —>- CH3OH + HCOOH

props.statement: Methanol forms from carbon dioxide and hydrogen by initial reduction of CO2 to CO with formation of water, reaction of hydrogen with CO to formaldehyde, and conversion of formaldehyde, in the presence of amphoteric aluminum oxide, to methanol and formic acid by the Cannizzaro reaction (2HCHO + H2O → CH3OH + HCOOH); the formic acid decomposes to H2 + CO2 or H2O + CO.

props.name: two paths: direct hydrogenation of formaldehyde and the Cannizzaro reaction
props.statement: After reduction of carbon dioxide through carbon monoxide to the formaldehyde stage, part of the methanol is formed by direct hydrogenation of the formaldehyde and part by the Cannizzaro reaction.

props.name: water formed from CO2 reduction, or CO2 itself, hinders ether formation
props.statement: The presence of water formed on reduction of carbon dioxide, or the carbon dioxide itself, may hinder the formation of methyl ether, explaining why no dimethyl ether forms from CO2 and hydrogen.

props.name: methanol formed came from actual synthesis (blank)
props.statement: With no catalyst in the reactor no condensate was obtained, showing that the small amounts of methanol formed were due to actual synthesis.

props.name: none of the catalysts was specific for methanol synthesis
props.statement: None of the catalysts used was specific for the reaction CO + 2H2 = CH3OH.

props.name: condensates essentially methanol and water
props.statement: Fractionation of the combined water layers of all condensates gave 1.6 cc. of methanol (b.p. 64°) with no appreciable n-propanol, so the condensates were essentially methanol and water; the oil layer (initial b.p. 102°) contained no methanol.

props.name: the earlier paper's equations give only order-of-magnitude Kp
props.note: concerns the authors' own earlier paper (This Journal, 55, 4747 (1933))
props.statement: Because the thermal data for formaldehyde are so doubtful, the equations of the authors' earlier paper give only order-of-magnitude values, and Kp for methanol synthesis derived from them would be far less accurate than direct measurement.

props.name: equation D best represents the measured points

evidence.quote: The agree- ment between the averages for a given temperature of the values measured in this work and equation D seems excellent, as shown in Table III

props.statement: The averages measured in this work agree excellently with equation D, and since D fits the other investigators' values as well as any of the equations, it appears to be the best representation of the points.

props.name: equation D is largely empirical
props.statement: Equation D must be regarded largely as an empirical equation which best represents the experimental points.

props.name: the fit of D is no proof of its thermal data
props.statement: That equation D fits the experimental points better than the other equations is no proof of the greater accuracy of its thermal data; e.g. D uses Thomsen's heat of combustion of CO, whereas Rossini's value is believed more accurate.

props.name: catalyst temperature uniform and steady within 0.1°

evidence.quote: The temperature throughout the catalyst did not vary more than 0.1° from the figure given in Table II as shown by calibrated thermo- couples placed at different locations in the cata- lyst bed.

props.statement: The temperature throughout the catalyst bed did not vary more than 0.1° from the Table II figure, nor with time more than 0.1°.

props.name: an alternative methanol heat capacity changes the curves only slightly
props.statement: The molal heat capacity of methanol vapour is somewhat in doubt, but using Francis's equation changes the location and slope of the curves only very slightly.

props.name: colorimetric and titration methods agree
props.statement: The excellent checks between the colorimetric and titration methods for methanol further indicate the absence of compounds other than methanol and water.

props.name: closer agreement requires a much more specific catalyst
props.statement: Closer agreement among measured values of the methanol equilibrium constant appears impossible until a much more specific catalyst is found.

props.name: methyl formate absent from the condensates
props.note: how it was shown is not described in this paper
props.statement: Methyl formate was shown to be absent from the condensates.

props.name: the 3 atm pressure correction (1.5% at 250°) is negligible
props.statement: The deviation of the equilibrium constant at three atmospheres from Kp0 is 1.5% at 250°, negligible compared with experimental errors, so no pressure correction was applied.

props.name: measured values at 225-275° and 3 atm agree with equation D

props.name: equilibrium bracketed from decomposition and synthesis sides

evidence.quote: Our method was first to pass pure methanol vapor over an active catalyst at a rate slow enough to give substantially equilibrium conditions.
This set a maximum value on the constant of the reaction.
Second, a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen was passed over the catalysts at a rate slow enough to give the maximum yield of methanol.
The latter experi- ment set a minimum limit on the value of the constant.
The vapor pressure of methanol at this tempera- ture was still over 40 times the equilibrium pressure, so that the experi- ments were thus started definitely on the methanol side of equilibrium.

props.statement: Passing methanol-containing gas over the catalyst sets a maximum value of the constant and passing the CO-H2 mixture sets a minimum value; the experiments were started definitely on the methanol side of equilibrium, at nearly equal distance from equilibrium in decomposition and synthesis.

Christiansen’s data are fairly close to ours.

give a constant more than 100 times this value.

props.name: series A particle surfaces are enriched in chromic acid
props.statement: In catalysts A the chromic-acid-rich liquid of the paste left, on drying, a surface layer of higher chromic acid content, so the particle surface is richer in chromic acid than the interior and the bulk composition of A does not indicate the real surface concentration; the composition of B does, since B is made from the solid free of liquid.

props.name: activity rises to an asymptotic maximum at Cr/Zn 0.5 (series B)
props.statement: Only series B (made from the solid free of liquid) gives the correct relation of composition to activity: activity rises with chromic acid content to an asymptotic maximum at Cr/Zn = 0.5; series A shows maximum synthesis activity at a Cr/Zn a little below 0.5, and B-10 (Cr/Zn 0.5) is more active than A-7 of the same ratio.

props.name: low-Cr catalysts are contaminated by carbon from CO decomposition
props.statement: Catalysts without or with a little chromic acid turned gray after a few days of synthesis and then gave far lower methanol-decomposition activity, whereas those with higher chromic acid content neither darkened nor lost activity: the surface of the former is more easily contaminated with carbon from carbon monoxide decomposition during the synthesis.

props.name: chromic acid improves selectivity and prevents CO decomposition
props.statement: Within the range studied, hardly any effect of chromic acid addition undesirable to the selectivity of the synthesis was found; by-products were very small (CO2 increase ≤ 1%, hardly any methane, formaldehyde 0.1%, methyl formate 0.5%), and the water yield, highest on the zinc oxide catalyst, falls rapidly with Cr/Zn. The authors emphasize the improvement of selectivity and the prevention of carbon monoxide decomposition by chromic acid, suggestive of an intracrystalline promoting effect.

props.name: nitrate coprecipitation gave no homogeneous, moderately active catalyst
props.statement: A catalyst prepared by coprecipitation of zinc and chromium hydroxides from a mixed nitrate solution proved difficult to obtain with homogeneous structure and moderate activity.

props.name: activity parallels surface area: intercrystalline promotion
props.statement: The catalytic activity of catalysts of different Cr/Zn almost parallels their specific surface area, and the activity per unit surface area changes far less than the activity per unit mass: this suggests an apparent proportionality of activity to surface area and, with the relation of surface area to Cr/Zn, an intercrystalline promoting effect of chromic acid.

props.name: chromic acid is also an intracrystalline promoter
props.statement: Chromic acid lowers both the frequency factor and the activation energy (per unit surface area) toward those of catalyst S, presumably a zinc chromite spinel, so the specific activity is maintained at the level of S; chromic acid behaves not only as an intercrystalline (structural) promoter but also as an intracrystalline promoter, modifying the catalyst structure advantageously for preserving the specific activity.

props.name: the maximum shortly before Cr/Zn 0.5 is not a necessary relation
props.statement: For that reason, the activity maximum at a Cr/Zn ratio shortly before 0.5, usual in previous work, is not the necessary relation between activity and chemical composition; an exact representation of the activity change in the intermediate range of Cr/Zn is not yet established.

props.name: paste solid holds at most Cr/Zn 0.5
props.statement: The solid in the paste (catalyst B) can contain no more chromic acid than that equivalent to Cr/Zn = 0.5; it is in equilibrium with a liquid of higher chromic acid concentration whose amount increases with the chromic acid content of the paste (paste 1/3 to 2.0: solid 0.31 to 0.50, liquid 0.82 to 1.95). Two hours of kneading at most complete the reaction and give a solid of homogeneous structure.

props.name: surface area max at Cr/Zn 0.4 in A; B larger than A
props.statement: In series A the specific surface area (after synthesis) passes through a maximum at Cr/Zn = 0.4; the catalysts of series B have larger specific surface areas than the corresponding ones of series A.

The trends of activation energy and frequency factor may be considered inherent to the clean surface although the syntheses were not always on a clean surface.

props.statement: An excessive addition of chromic acid may certainly decrease the activity, since chromic acid alone is no more an active catalyst than zinc oxide alone.

props.name: activity falls after heating and after use
props.statement: The activity is high immediately after reduction of the raw catalyst at 250 °C and becomes lower after heating at 360 and 450 °C for two hours; the activity after synthesis runs 1-10 lies even lower than after heating at 450 °C.

props.name: axial temperature and concentration profiles
props.statement: The bed temperature remains below the oil bath temperature in the top zone, rises rapidly in the intermediate zone and, after a maximum, decreases slowly in the bottom zone; the methanol concentration is extremely low in the top zone, begins to rise in the intermediate zone and rises more slowly until the equilibrium concentration is attained at the bottom of the bed.

props.name: calculated profiles almost consistent
props.statement: Calculated average-temperature profiles for Exps. 1, 7 and 9 are almost, though not entirely, consistent with the experimental ones, which may be the order of accuracy to be expected of the performance data; calculated radial profiles agree well near the top of the third step, with a discrepancy increasing with bed length.

props.name: earlier reaction-heat formulae do not fit
props.statement: None of the earlier formulae for the axial reaction-heat distribution (Q = q0 e^-cx, Q = A e^-cx + B, Q = c1 e^-Mx + c2 e^-Nx) could express the present axial distribution data of the reaction heat.

props.name: start-up ignition risk
props.statement: Particularly at the beginning of the synthesis, a sudden temperature rise in the catalyst bed must be avoided because it would cause ignition of the catalyst granules.

props.name: outer tube surface resistance largest
props.statement: The heat transfer resistance is largest at the outer tube surface.

props.name: product impurities small
props.statement: The synthesis product contains only 1-3% water and 0-0.3% methyl formate as impurities; very little carbon dioxide or methane was detected in the exit gas.

props.name: radial temperature rise grows as H2/CO falls

evidence.quote: The temperature rise over a cross section of the catalyst bed reaches as high as about 40•Ž in the bottom zone.

props.statement: The radial temperature profile is concave upwards at the top of the bed, flat in the intermediate zone and convex upwards in the lower zone; the temperature rise over a cross section reaches about 40 °C in the bottom zone, and within the range of operating conditions its magnitude increases with a decreasing ratio of hydrogen to carbon monoxide.

props.name: STY rises with flow rate and with lower H2/CO
props.statement: The space-time yield of the reactor is rather lower than usual with commercial reactors; it becomes higher as the flow rate of the inlet gas is increased or as the ratio of hydrogen to carbon monoxide is decreased.

props.name: improve outer heat transfer and control temperature rise
props.statement: For efficient reactor performance, not only should the heat transfer at the outer tube surface be improved, but the temperature rise in the catalyst bed should also be controlled by a suitable means.

props.name: top zone too cold, bottom zone too hot
props.statement: Compared with the maximum-rate curve, the temperature in the top zone of the catalyst bed (low methanol concentration) is too low and that in the bottom zone (high methanol concentration) too high for efficient performance of the reactor.

props.statement: The A reactor produced a much larger amount of methanol than the reactor with no heat exchanger (O reactor), its space-time yield reaching twice that of the O reactor (Exp. I vs Exp. 3), provided the synthesis gas was preheated at a higher temperature (Exps. 2 and 3).

props.name: B reactor smaller gain than A
props.statement: The B reactor also produced more methanol than the O reactor, but the increase was rather low compared with the A reactor (Exp. 1 vs Exp. 6).

props.statement: The Bcalcd values obtained with h from formulae A, C and E, and with h' from formula F, are consistent with the bed-averaged B̄exp.

props.name: bed resistance about one-third
props.statement: The heat transfer resistance across the catalyst bed is so high as to account for about one-third of the overall heat transfer resistance between the gas in the bed and the gas in the heat exchanger tube.

props.name: Bexp maximum near 0.4 m
props.statement: The experimental cooling coefficient Bexp differs with bed length, with a maximum at about x = 0.4 m.

props.name: C reactor overcools the bed
props.statement: Reliable performance data could not be collected with the C reactor until the incoming gas had been preheated to a much higher temperature (Exp. 7); in this reactor the heat exchanger tube cooled the catalyst bed so much that the bed temperature would decrease too low to allow the progress of the synthesis.

props.name: calculated A-reactor profiles agree
props.statement: The axial temperature profiles calculated for Exp. 4 accord well with the experimental ones, indicating that an adequate Bcalcd from any of the formulae proposed so far can be used for the profile calculation without serious errors.

props.name: profile maxima: upper half in A, bottom in B and C
props.statement: The temperature maximum appears in the upper half of the catalyst bed of the A reactor but near the bottom of the B and C reactors, whose catalyst-inlet temperature is kept considerably lower even with higher preheating; in the A reactor methanol is already produced in the top zone and increases rather monotonously with bed length, whereas in B and C only a small amount appears after more than a quarter of the bed; the B and C profiles are essentially the same in tendency as with the O reactor.

props.name: B/C second passage cools the inlet
props.statement: Owing to the efficient heat transfer between the gases in passages II and III, the temperature profile in the second passage of the B and C exchangers always slopes down markedly in the upper zone, and as a consequence the catalyst inlet temperature is kept comparatively low.

props.name: only the single-tube countercurrent exchanger raises production
props.statement: Among the single-tube countercurrent, double-tube countercurrent and double-tube concurrent heat exchanger tubes, only the first serves to increase methanol production considerably compared with the previously tested reactor with no heat exchanger tube.

props.name: CO oxidation by catalyst improbable
props.statement: Oxidation of CO by the catalyst was improbable because the catalyst had been thoroughly reduced at 250 °C, above the 180 °C reaction temperature, with the reactant gas, and no degradation of catalytic activity to form carbon dioxide was observed.

props.name: CO2 formation grows with temperature
props.statement: In preliminary experiments at 160-230 °C, carbon dioxide formation was remarkable at higher temperatures while the reaction rate was too slow to observe below 180 °C; the temperature coefficient was therefore not measured and the temperature fixed at 180 °C.

props.name: deviation at low n (protium)
props.statement: Systematic deviation from the fitted equations is observed in the lower range of n for only the protium series (for all l-m-s combinations); calculated lines for Eqs. 8-10 overlap and the experimental points lie along them apart from this.

props.name: Eq. 8 abandoned
props.note: the 'established fact of pressure dependency' is the authors' premise from the literature, not a test of this source
props.statement: Estimated at elevated pressures, Eq. 8 gives a rate independent of pressure above 20 atm (Eqs. 9 and 10 do not); this contradicts the established pressure dependency of methanol synthesis, so Eq. 8 may be abandoned.

props.name: isotope effect in CO2 formation
props.statement: An isotope effect was found in the carbon dioxide formation at higher concentrations of carbon monoxide; the CO2 formed was near 20 mol% of the methanol in most runs, at most 30%.

props.name: no H/D isotope effect on methanol formation
props.statement: No deuterium isotope effect was observed in methanol synthesis: protium and deuterium points lie along the same line with no systematic deviation (Figs. 2 and 3), confirmed by changing the reactant gases in the order H-D-H-D-D.

props.name: no methane: path ii excluded
props.statement: Methane was absent from the circulating gas after several hours of reaction (gas chromatography), so the path 2CO + 2H2 = CO2 + CH4 was excluded.

props.name: rate equation not uniquely determined
props.statement: The range of experimental conditions was not wide enough to discriminate a single rate equation; the three equations reached all have adsorption terms of both hydrogen and carbon monoxide, as in the equation of Natta et al., with a different exponent s.

props.name: rM independent of space velocity
props.statement: No marked influence on rM was observed on changing the space velocity from 900 to 1800.

props.name: optimum n about 2

evidence.quote: The optimum methanol formation appears at a n value of around 2.

props.statement: The optimum methanol formation appears at an H2/CO (or D2/CO) ratio n of around 2 at 180 °C and 1 atm.

props.statement: For Eq. 9 the reaction scheme may be H2 = 2H(a) (III), CO + 2H(a) -> CH2O(a) (IV), CH2O(a) + H(a) -> CH3O(a) (V), CH3O(a) + H(a) -> CH3OH (VI), with reaction V rate-determining.

props.name: CO adsorption rate-determining (view the authors reject)
props.statement: The absence of an isotope effect on methanol formation may give rise to the view that the adsorption of carbon monoxide is rate-determining.

props.name: CO2 formation on a site different from methanol formation
props.statement: The hydrogen isotope effect in CO2 formation, observed especially at higher CO concentrations where the methanol rate also deviates from the rate equation, may suggest that CO2 formation takes place on an active site different from that of methanol formation.

props.name: CO + H2 -> HCHO; HCHO + H2 -> CH3OH, reaction II rate-determining
props.statement: If methanol synthesis consists of CO + H2 -> HCHO (I) and HCHO + H2 -> CH3OH (II), Eq. 10 conforms to reaction II being rate-determining, because the partial pressure of HCHO is then K_I pH2 pCO.

props.name: rate-determining step involves hydrogen
props.statement: The rate equations suggest a rate-determining step in which hydrogen or a hydrogen-containing species is involved; reconciling this with the absent isotope effect requires further investigation.

props.name: methanol has no effect on rM under these conditions
props.statement: Since the variation in space velocity should give a different methanol vapor pressure in the catalyst bed, it seems that methanol has no effect on rM under the present conditions; the adsorption term of methanol may disappear because of the low conversion.

props.name: adsorbed H2/CO independent of gas phase
props.statement: The composition of the adsorbed phase (H2(a)/CO(a)) did not depend on that of the gas phase in spite of an about eight-thousand-fold change of the partial pressure ratio, in synthesis with and without the liquid-nitrogen trap and in methanol decomposition.

props.name: rate equation agrees with Uchida-Ogino
props.note: Eq. 2 and its conditions are cited from Uchida and Ogino (ref. 5), not measured in this source
props.statement: Eq. 1 (n = 0.75) is in good agreement with the equation r = k(PH2²PCO)^(1−α), α = 0.3, previously reported by Uchida and Ogino, in spite of their different conditions (300-360 °C, 90-150 kg/cm2 vs 250 °C, 100-760 mmHg).

props.name: Langmuir-type adsorption inappropriate
props.note: the authors also cite Uchida and Ogino (ref. 12) that the rate cannot be expressed by any Langmuir-type equation; that is a cited result
props.statement: The rate equations could be read as a partially covered surface with Langmuir-type adsorption, but considerable amounts of adsorption are involved (Table I), so applying Langmuir-type adsorption seems inappropriate.

props.name: methanol far below equilibrium
props.statement: The amounts of methanol formed were far less than those calculated from the equilibrium constant and from the circulating rate.

props.name: H2 and CO adsorption mutually enhanced
props.statement: The amounts of hydrogen and carbon monoxide adsorbed during the reaction were greater than those adsorbed separately with the corresponding amounts introduced, indicating a marked mutual influence on the adsorption of each gas in the presence of the other; adsorption during the reaction cannot be estimated from results in the absence of the other gas.

props.name: products methanol and CO2
props.statement: The observed products were usually methanol and carbon dioxide and, depending on the conditions, small amounts of water and a trace of methane.

props.name: results reproducible with evacuation before each run
props.statement: With the catalyst evacuated for 3 hr at 400 °C before each run, the experimental results were satisfactorily reproducible.

props.name: water vapor kept from contaminating the catalyst
props.note: the source states the precaution only; it reports no measured effect of water vapor on the catalyst
props.statement: When the circulating rate was measured with a soap-film meter connected through stop-cocks I and J, precautions were taken to prevent water vapor from contaminating the catalyst.

props.statement: The Eley-Rideal-type hydrogenation of the CH3O surface complex by gaseous hydrogen is the rate-determining step of methanol synthesis (the authors 'conclude' it may be so; the Summary says it 'has been suggested').

props.name: air decomposition endothermic at ca. 310 °C, unlike exothermic decomposition in synthesis gas

evidence.note: The exothermic decomposition in synthesis gas from 200 °C is cited from Kawamura and Irie.; quote withheld: sha256:c65a744f9d0b849048dfa037da3d60c3bf91590e38ae457e916dd2e6c724e7eb chars:245
continues on p. 6: 'trivalent oxide, which combines with zinc oxide to form zinc chromite.'; quote withheld: sha256:8e5212878d5fdecce86c8ef9a846caa885b588d2599972d724903969cf50e0eb chars:93

props.note: The 200 °C exothermic decomposition in synthesis gas is cited, not measured here.
props.statement: The hydroxychromate of A0-3 decomposes in air endothermically at about 310 °C, a different type from the decomposition in synthesis gas (exothermic, from about 200 °C according to Kawamura and Irie); the endothermic peak is due to the conversion of sexivalent chromium oxide by oxygen removal into the trivalent oxide, which combines with zinc oxide to form zinc chromite.

props.name: air heating lowers k'; main reason B is less active
props.statement: k' depends on Cr/Zn nearly as k does. In series A both high k' and moderately large S give the high k; in series B k' is the sole factor, S being nearly equal for all. Heating the chromium-containing catalysts in air at 400 °C lowers k' considerably, and since the air-heated catalysts have larger surface areas after synthesis, this decrease in k' is the main reason why series B is less active.

props.name: by-products at 380 °C

evidence.quote: 13) The percentages are based on the weight of the liquid product. In no cases was isobutanol detectable.

props.statement: In the liquid products at 380 °C, dimethyl ether (0.7-1.5%), methyl formate (0.5-0.6%) and formaldehyde (0.1%) are nearly independent of catalyst or chromium content; water is said to be higher with lower-activity catalysts (5% for A-3, 1.1% for A-1, as printed); isobutanol was never detectable.

props.name: zinc chromite lattice larger than normal; ZnO normal
props.note: The literature values are cited (A.S.T.M. data file).
props.statement: The zinc oxide lattice constants vary little and agree with the literature value (3.249 Å); the zinc chromite lattice constants of the catalysts (8.397-8.523 Å) are generally greater than the literature values (8.32, 8.20 Å) and stay enlarged after prolonged heating in hydrogen at 500 °C.

props.name: the two series differ structurally under the electron microscope
props.statement: Reduction of A0-3 produces caterpillar-like particles about 50 Å wide (aggregates of ca. 50 Å crystallites) within the fringe of the hydroxychromate crystal, which grow with gaps during synthesis (probably sintering); the air-heated B0-3 resembles A0-3 and B1-3 stays mostly homogeneous; heating in hydrogen at 500 °C causes marked crystal growth, more in B1-3.

props.name: hydroxychromates decompose to ZnO and zinc chromite
props.statement: Original A0-2 contains hydroxychromate IIIβ with zinc oxide, A0-3 hydroxychromate Iβ alone, and the highest-chromium catalyst an unidentified pattern; after reduction in synthesis gas or use in synthesis only zinc oxide and zinc chromite are seen, so the hydroxychromates have decomposed; heating in air at 400 °C also decomposes them (B0), B0-4 showing unidentified intermediates.

props.name: optimum Cr/Zn 0.5; unheated series A more active than air-heated B
props.statement: The optimum chromium/zinc atomic ratio is 0.5 in each series, and every catalyst of series A (not heated in air) is more active than the corresponding catalyst of series B (heated in air at 400 °C, 5 h), although series A has much smaller surface areas after synthesis (k330: A-3 17.9×10^-2, B-3 15.2×10^-2 atm^-2.1 hr^-1).

props.name: BET-derived particle size disagrees with electron microscopy
props.statement: The average particle diameter d = 6/ρtS differs greatly from the sizes seen by electron microscopy (e.g. A0-3: about 4000 Å cube vs. thin plates of several thousand Å; A2-3: 160 Å vs. caterpillars about 50 Å wide); the discrepancies of A0-3 and A2-3 are explained by particle shape, that of B1-3 cannot be explained satisfactorily, and d is of minor significance.

props.name: used-catalyst particles are aggregates of ZnO and chromite crystallites

evidence.quote: The residue from the sample A2-3 was found to have a chromium/zinc ratio of 1.79, which is approximately the ratio for zinc chromite.

props.statement: After removal of free zinc oxide the residue of A2-3 has Cr/Zn 1.79 (about that of zinc chromite) and looks essentially like the initial sample, so most particles of A2-3 are aggregates of zinc oxide and zinc chromite crystallites, the others zinc oxide alone or mainly; in B1-3 the residue shows wide openings, so the two components are locally concentrated and their mutual penetration is less thorough than in A2-3.

props.name: series A more thermally stable
props.statement: Comparing A-3 with A'-3 and B-3 with B'-3 (after 8 h in hydrogen at 500 °C) gives an approximate concept of relative thermal stability; series A is the more thermally stable. Heating for only 2 h in hydrogen lowered activity as much as 8 h.

props.name: surface area depends on treatment history
props.statement: Original chromium-containing catalysts (A0) have very small surface areas, smaller than the zinc oxide catalyst; reduction in synthesis gas enlarges them 30-50 times; use in synthesis then lowers them, the more the lower the chromium content. Air heating at 400 °C slightly increases them; after synthesis the air-heated catalysts (B1) have larger areas than A2, nearly the same for all chromium contents. Heating in hydrogen at 500 °C for 8 h after synthesis markedly decreases the area, more for B1-3. Helium density decreases with chromium content; particles of the original catalysts are large and split into very fine particles on reduction.
