h2_co_ratio.as_reported: 2H2-1CO

props.name: reactants reach a coherent surface smaller than the particle surface
props.statement: The surface of all particles estimated from micrographs can exceed the BET area; following Nielsen, interfacial layers coalesce into a coherent surface, and this coherent surface, which the reactants reach, should be used in interpreting k through specific activity and surface area.

props.name: slow decomposition in synthesis gas vs. sudden decomposition in air
props.statement: The structural difference between the series may stem from how zinc hydroxychromate decomposes: in synthesis gas slowly but more completely (excess oxygen removed as CO2), fine ZnO and zinc chromite crystallites forming at low temperature and serving as nuclei for large particles in which the two interpenetrate thoroughly; in air suddenly at 310 °C, into very fine crystallites scattered in the fringe of the layer structure with incomplete oxygen removal, a structure hard to transform later in synthesis gas.

props.name: specific activity follows ZnO-chromite interpenetration, not lattice constant
props.statement: The specific activity cannot be correlated with the zinc chromite lattice constant (which varies little while k' differs greatly between series); the difference in specific activity is attributed to the degree of mutual penetration of zinc oxide and zinc chromite, consistent with the rise of B'-3's specific activity to the level of A-3 after heating in hydrogen at 500 °C, which favours that penetration.

props.name: excess Zn2+ in interstices of non-stoichiometric chromite enlarges its lattice
props.statement: Taking Irie and Shiraishi's view (low-temperature chromite occludes zinc oxide), where the zinc chromite is non-stoichiometric, Zn2+ enters the empty interstices, enlarging and stressing the lattice. The broadening of the chromite lines after removal of the excess zinc oxide is probably due to the stress this removal imposes.

props.name: about 60 % of feed CO carbon goes to methanol
props.statement: From the carbon balance of feed and exit gas, the carbon distribution of the feed CO to CH3OH is 59.5 %, i.e. nearly 60 %.

props.name: copper strongly promotes the zinc catalyst, maximum near Zn66.6Cu33.3

evidence.note: Figure 1: carbon distribution to CO (%) vs. catalyst composition, Zn 100 → Cu 100 mol %; plots the Table 1 values
evidence.quote: 第1図亜鉛触媒に対する銅の

props.statement: Zinc alone gives only 27.4 % carbon distribution to CO at 280 °C, but copper has a marked promoter action: Zn75Cu25 (25 mol % Cu) gives 87.9 % and Zn66.6Cu33.3 gives 89.5 %; with more Cu the activity falls again (Zn50Cu50 68.5 %), falls sharply above 50 mol % Cu, and Cu alone gives only 1.0 %.

props.name: the catalyst brings methanol synthesis fairly close to equilibrium

evidence.note: image reads: from the ΔF° equation of Parks and Huffman ΔF° = −17,660 + 17.5 T ln T − 0.0136 T² − 57.2 T, ΔF°543 = 7120, Kp = 3.25×10^-4, and the conversion of CO to CH3OH at 270 °C, 200 atm is 77 %; quote withheld: sha256:22f8f9227cdf94549ef68aa0fe972ad4d0e1375a2e6a5c156fa03adfd08a1828 chars:243

image reads: taking 59.5 % as the equilibrium value, with fugacities of H2 ≈ CO ≈ 210 atm and CH3OH ≈ 90 atm at 270 °C, 200 atm (ref. 4), Kpo = pfCH3OH/(pfH2²·pfCO) = 0.71×10^-4, somewhat smaller than the average of the many reported Kp values; quote withheld: sha256:067e0060a2a3083ccb87d76cafa0eb233f16f76af55ee2b96562a1f6c484f2f3 chars:224

props.statement: Compared with the equilibrium conversion of CO to CH3OH of 77 % at 270 °C and 200 atm (from Parks and Huffman's ΔF° equation), the observed 59.5 % shows that at least under these conditions the Zn75Cu25(ThO2)3 catalyst takes the methanol synthesis considerably close to equilibrium.

props.name: the liquid product is nearly pure methanol
props.statement: The liquid product is colourless and transparent, d20/4 = 0.792; 81.7 % distils at 64.0–66.0 °C and 16.6 % at 66.0–68.0 °C, with no higher-boiling fraction, so it can be regarded as almost pure methanol.

props.name: desulfurized water gas mixed with electrolytic hydrogen
props.description: Water gas mixed with electrolytic hydrogen: CO 35.8 %, H2 52.4 % (CO:H2 = 1:1.464), CO2 2.0 %, O2 0.4 %, CnH2n (n=2) 0.2 %, CH4 1.4 %, N2 7.8 %, S 0.85 g/100 m3. The raw water gas was desulfurized by sodium carbonate washing, catalytic decomposition of organic sulfur over an Fe:Al:diatomaceous earth catalyst at 200–250 °C and Thylox washing, to a sulfur content of 1.0 g/100 m3 or less.

air-dried at 105 °C in an electric drier and powdered

props.statement: Under the conditions of (1)-(10), with about 25 % CO2 in the feed the reaction rate is negligibly low; lowering the CO2 fraction raises it somewhat but side reactions cannot be stopped, and the conditions are unsuitable for recirculation.

props.name: kieselguhr 200atm slight increase
props.statement: With the Mn-Cu catalyst plus 14 % kieselguhr at 200 atm and below 10 % CO2 in the feed, the methanol yield increased somewhat.

props.name: lower temperature by 100C very good
props.statement: Lowering the reaction temperature by about 100 °C relative to (1)-(10) gives very good results.

props.name: methanol analysis methods agree
props.statement: Methanol determined by acetylation (pyridine as auxiliary) and by calculation from the methanol-water specific-gravity table agreed well.

props.name: mn cu kieselguhr too much methane
props.statement: Methane formation is also very large, so from the standpoint of methanol production the Mn-Cu catalyst with kieselguhr is hardly worth considering.

props.name: mn cu scarcely reacts 320 350
props.statement: With the Mn-Cu catalyst at 320-350 °C, 150 atm and space velocity near 4,500 there is almost no reaction, and it tends to produce more methane than carbon monoxide.

props.name: mn cu slight reaction 370 400
props.statement: Raising the temperature to 370-400 °C and lowering the space velocity gives a slight reaction on the Mn-Cu catalyst.

props.name: optimum temperature 250 260
props.note: the discussion says 'seems to be' (思われる); the summary states it; the comparison is with the cited results of Sakikawa et al.
props.statement: For the equimolar Zn, Cu catalyst the optimum reaction temperature, sought in (13)-(16), is 250-260 °C; this is more than 100 °C lower than the optimum (350-400 °C) found by Sakikawa et al.

props.name: recirculation co2 decays co to methane

evidence.quote: ガスを循環している間に,炭酸ガスの量は対数曲線的に減少し一旦生じた一酸化炭素は,漸次メタンに変化して行くのが見られる,

props.statement: During recirculation (Figure 1, run 10) the amount of carbon dioxide decreases along a logarithmic curve, and carbon monoxide once formed gradually changes to methane; carbon monoxide changes to methane even more than to methanol.

props.name: recirculation increases methanol yield
props.statement: Runs (9) and (10) show that recirculating the gas increases the methanol yield.

props.name: space velocity can be high

evidence.quote: (12)では同じ触媒を50ccだけを使つて空間速度60・000近くで行つても2$%の変化率を示し,空間速度を相当早く出来る。ことを示した』

props.note: the text layer prints '2$%'; the printed page and Table 1 read 23 % (23.4)
props.statement: Run (12), with only 50 cc of the same catalyst at a space velocity near 60,000, still gave 23 % conversion, showing that the space velocity can be made considerably high.

props.name: summary space velocity 15000
props.note: the comparison is with the cited results of Sakikawa et al.
props.statement: Fully satisfactory results are obtained even at space velocities of 15,000 and above, far larger than the 2,400 that Sakikawa et al. found optimal.

props.name: summary zn cu 50 50 best
props.note: the agreement is with the cited work of Sakikawa et al.
props.statement: Among the catalysts tried, Zn:Cu = 50:50 (mole ratio) gave the best results; this agrees with the results of Sakikawa et al.

props.name: co inhibits reaction
props.statement: Since conversion to methanol in (14) is lower than in (15), much carbon monoxide seems to inhibit the reaction; even if it does not inhibit, CO formation here is better regarded as a purely side reaction.

props.name: co2 to methanol via co
props.statement: Because the methanol yield is higher when the feed contains a few per cent of carbon monoxide, under these conditions carbon dioxide may be converted to methanol by way of carbon monoxide.

props.name: higher pressure and h2 partial pressure raise conversion
props.note: the author also cites the Commercial Solvents process (CO2:H2 = 1:9) in support; cited, not this source's result
props.statement: Methanol formation is in general better the higher the pressure, and the conversion of carbon dioxide to methanol should increase with higher hydrogen partial pressure; hence 200 atm and less than 10 % CO2 in the feed were used with the kieselguhr catalyst.

props.name: zn cu better than mn cu undecided
props.statement: Considering various conditions the Zn-Cu system appears superior to the Mn-Cu system, but comparison of (1)-(7) with (8) alone does not settle this; it needs further study.

props.method: co-precipitation
steps: a mixed aqueous solution of the nitrates of each metal (as far as possible) is boiled
caustic alkali is added to precipitate simultaneously
the support is added during precipitation and stirred in
washed by decantation and dried
the dried powder is calcined once at about 300 °C and then shaped

props.name: high-pressure reaction tower with compressor, preheater and high-pressure separator
props.description: Feed gas from a gas holder passes a water separator and gas meter, is compressed to 150-200 atm, freed of oil, preheated to about 200 °C, reacted in the tower held at temperature, cooled, and methanol is separated in a high-pressure separator. In recirculation runs the exit gas is expanded to atmospheric pressure through an expansion valve and returned ahead of the compressor (no circulating pump).

props.statement: The X-ray pattern of a domestic commercial 'Zinc chromate' is a mixture of (A) and (B), not true ZnCrO4; the spacings Hanawalt gives for 'ZnCrO4' are exactly those of (B), not of ZnCrO4.

evidence.quote: この反面Cr20$の 線が強 大となって600℃ ではほとんど完全なCr203と なる6

props.statement: Products of CrO3 calcined at 250 °C or below are too hygroscopic to photograph; after the decomposition near 300 °C they are not hygroscopic. At 355 and 450 °C they contain lines of neither CrO3 nor Cr2O3, which weaken at higher temperature while the Cr2O3 lines grow, giving almost complete Cr2O3 at 600 °C.

props.name: CrO3 decomposes via Cr2O5 to Cr2O3
props.note: 'Cr205' and 'Cr盆03' are the text layer's renderings of Cr2O5 and Cr2O3
props.statement: The thermobalance results for CrO3 alone agree fairly well with those of Honda and Vasenin and show that CrO3 becomes Cr2O3 via Cr2O5.

props.name: assignment of the CrO3 thermal changes
props.statement: Chromic anhydride alone shows five marked changes E, F, G, H and I: E is the release of free water, G, H and I correspond to the decompositions C, D and E of Fig. 1, and F is the endothermic heat of fusion at the melting point of chromic anhydride, without weight change.

props.name: thermal changes are irreversible

evidence.quote: いずれの試料も温度の上昇に伴なって分解が起るが,温 度を降 下する際は変化はいずれも認められず,し たがって不可逆変化で ある。

props.statement: In every sample decomposition occurs as the temperature rises, but no change is seen on cooling, so the changes are irreversible; zinc oxide alone shows no thermal change.

props.name: B, C and D series of thermal changes for Zn/Cr > 1
props.statement: For Zn/Cr > 1, apart from A of 1.5:1, there are a B series of changes from about 270-280 °C, a C series at about 320-330 °C and a D series near 480 °C; the B series is largest at 4:1, the C series at 2:1, and the D series grows as Cr increases. The two different decompositions (B, C) were not clearly discernible in the thermobalance curves.

props.name: excess CrO3 is mixed in its original form
props.statement: At Zn:Cr = 1:5 the decompositions corresponding to G and I are clearly seen and at 1:2 no marked change; the trend differs clearly from Zn/Cr > 1, and it is almost certain that the excess chromic anhydride is mixed in its original form.

props.name: B and C are dehydrations, D a deoxygenation following 2CrO3 = Cr2O3 + 3/2 O2
props.statement: The products of the thermal changes are: A dehydration, B and C series dehydration, D series deoxygenation; the oxygen released equals the amount calculated for decomposition of the added chromic anhydride by 2CrO3 = Cr2O3 + 3/2 O2, and the water of the B and C series corresponds to 4ZnO·CrO3·3H2O at 4:1 and 2ZnO·CrO3·H2O at 2:1.

props.name: calcination at 700 °C gives ZnCr2O4 spinel

evidence.quote: これは ZnCr慧04(spi難e1)で あって

props.note: the comparison with coprecipitated catalysts refers to cited work (ref. 9)
props.statement: After calcination at 700 °C for 2 h, Zn:Cr = 1:2 shows the characteristic lines of ZnCr2O4 spinel, as with catalysts prepared from coprecipitates; with more zinc, ZnO lines appear besides the spinel, and with more chromium, Cr2O3 lines appear (Table 3). This proves that oxygen is released according to equation (1) and chromium goes from hexavalent to trivalent.

props.name: summary: 4:1 and 2:1 hydrates lose water and oxygen endothermically
props.statement: For Zn/Cr >= 1, the 4:1 and 2:1 materials have definite X-ray structures corresponding to 4ZnO·CrO3·3H2O and 2ZnO·CrO3·H2O; the crystal water of the former is released endothermically at 270-280 °C and of the latter at 320-330 °C, and at 470-480 °C endothermic deoxygenation releases the oxygen corresponding to 2CrO3 -> Cr2O3 + 3/2 O2. Above Zn/Cr = 1 in Cr, excess CrO3 appears to be mixed as it is; after 700 °C, 2 h, Zn:Cr = 1:2 forms the spinel, with ZnO lines when Zn is richer and Cr2O3 lines when Cr is richer.

props.name: thermal decomposition in air differs for Zn/Cr > 1, = 1 and < 1

evidence.quote: 370◎C付 近で新に特異な分解を起す.

props.statement: On heating in air, catalysts with Zn/Cr > 1 decompose near 300 °C and near 500 °C with nearly the same trend; Zn/Cr = 1 shows decomposition at 150-200 °C and a very broad decomposition from about 400 to 550 °C; Zn/Cr < 1 shows a new decomposition near 370 °C; zinc oxide alone loses no weight up to 650 °C; CrO3 alone shows three decompositions between about 270 and 470 °C.

props.name: Zn:Cr = 1:1 divides the catalysts into two systems
props.statement: The catalysts divide at Zn:Cr = 1:1 into two systems: for Zn/Cr > 1 the decomposition curves appear in neither zinc oxide nor chromic anhydride, so they cannot be simple mixtures; for Zn/Cr <= 1 the curves approach that of chromic anhydride alone as more is added, so the chromic anhydride in excess of Zn:Cr = 1:1 is mixed in as it is.

props.name: only 4:1 and 2:1 have a definite X-ray structure

evidence.quote: その反面新たな午渉線(A)が 次第に強くなり,Zn:Cr=411に おいて酸価匪鉛の線は完全に 消滅し,(A)の 干渉線のみとなる。

props.note: the ratios are printed '1.4:1' and '211' in the garbled text layer; read as 4:1 and 2:1
props.statement: In the uncalcined catalysts the zinc oxide lines weaken with increasing Cr while new lines (A) strengthen, and at Zn:Cr = 4:1 only (A) remains; with more Cr (A) weakens and (B) strengthens, strongest at 2:1; with still more Cr lines (C), thought to be a dichromate, appear. Of the Zn/Cr >= 1 catalysts only 4:1 and 2:1 are zinc chromates of definite X-ray structure; the other compositions are merely mixtures of these.

props.note: stated as a premise; no synthesis test is reported in this paper
props.statement: As methanol-synthesis catalysts, compositions richer in zinc than chromium are effective, so mainly these were measured by X-ray.

props.name: the recalculation with Pasquon's equation agrees well with the plant measurements (final conversion 4.3% calculated vs 3.6% measured; wall temperatures)
props.statement: The recalculation of the Leuna converter with Pasquon's kinetic equation agrees well with the operating measurements: the calculated final conversion of 4.3% is higher than the measured 3.6%, and the furnace wall temperatures agree, supporting the use of Pasquon's equation for reactors with the Leuna catalyst.

props.name: highest temperatures can lie in the lower third of the converter (confirms plant observation)
props.statement: The calculated temperature profile confirms the plant observation that the highest temperatures can lie in the lower third of the converter, explained by the different cold-gas amounts and layer heights with an almost linear increase of conversion.

props.name: the inflection of the temperature profile between cold-gas feeds lies where the rate is maximal; the 2nd cold-gas amount was much too small
props.statement: Between two cold-gas injections the temperature profile has an inflection point where the reaction rate reaches its maximum; the second cold-gas amount was much too small, so the temperature of maximum rate was not reached in that section and the rate fell continuously.

props.name: inlet temperature of the first stage too low and of the third too high: layer heights wrongly designed
props.statement: The recalculation showed that the inlet temperature of the first stage is too low and that of the third stage too high; both stages were controlled so that the outlet approaches the permitted 400 °C. The unfavourable inlet temperatures are ultimately due to a wrong design of the catalyst layer heights.

props.statement: Because the rates were referred to catalyst weight and the Leuna catalyst's mean bulk density is 1.60 g/cm3 against about 0.85 g/cm3 for the Montecatini catalyst, the Leuna converter does almost twice as much per reactor volume as Natta's test reactor.

props.name: in practice temperatures of about 400 °C must not be exceeded because strongly exothermic methane formation sets in
props.statement: In practice temperatures of about 400 °C must not be exceeded, since otherwise the strongly exothermic methane formation occurs; only a limited number of cold-gas lines can be fitted, and at higher methanol concentrations the rate maxima move to lower temperatures.

props.name: at 7.1 m bed height no limit is reached; a longer converter would raise conversion appreciably; reactor gives about 50% of equilibrium conversion

evidence.quote: schichthöhe von 7,1 m noch kein Grenzwert erreicht ist, d. h. eine Verlängerung

props.statement: At a catalyst height of 7.1 m the conversion has not reached a limiting value, so lengthening the converter would noticeably increase conversion; the equilibrium conversion at outlet conditions is about 7.5% methanol, so the reactor achieves only about 50% of the thermodynamically possible conversion.

props.name: the converter runs optimally when the inflection point lies about in the middle of a catalyst section
props.statement: Since the rate curves are roughly symmetric about their maximum, the reactor is run optimally under the given conditions when the inflection of the temperature profile lies about in the middle of a catalyst section.

props.name: Pasquon (cited): rate governed by third-order surface reactions with atomic hydrogen; on ZnO-Cr2O3 CO + 2H = CH2O and CH2O + 2H = CH3OH, on ZnO-Cr2O3-CuO only formaldehyde formation
props.note: cited from Pasquon (ref. 7) and Natta (ref. 5)
props.statement: According to Pasquon, the overall rate is determined by at least one third-order surface reaction in the adsorbed phase with hydrogen adsorbed atomically; on a ZnO-Cr2O3 contact two third-order reactions, CO + 2H = CH2O and CH2O + 2H = CH3OH, are rate-determining, whereas on a ZnO-Cr2O3-CuO contact only the formation of formaldehyde matters.

props.name: an experimental reactor for the kinetics with the Leuna catalyst is planned; further optimisation on the ZRA 1 computer
props.statement: Differences such as 3.6% measured versus 4.3% calculated conversion are of the order of the possible improvement in optimisation, so an experimental reactor for the kinetics of methanol synthesis with the Leuna catalyst is to be set up; further optimisation calculations will be done with the ZRA 1 computer.

props.statement: For the Leuna catalyst both reactions (CO + 2H = CH2O and CH2O + 2H = CH3OH) should determine the course of the overall process, so the other steps (adsorption of H2 and CO, desorption of methanol) can be treated as at equilibrium.

props.name: the Natta-Pasquon kinetic approach probably comes close to the real course of methanol catalysis
props.statement: Since Natta's adsorption enthalpies from the temperature dependence of the adsorption constants agreed well with calorimetric heats, the kinetic approach of Natta and Pasquon probably comes close to the real course of the methanol catalysis.

props.name: similar conversions with 0.6-0.9 mm grains and 5-9 mm pellets suggest pore diffusion has little influence (conclusion called risky)
props.statement: The approximately equal conversions with 0.6-0.9 mm grains in Natta's test reactor and 5 mm and 9 mm pellets in the Leuna reactor suggest that the reaction is only slightly influenced by pore diffusion; given the different preparation of the two catalysts, conclusions on the mechanism on the Leuna catalyst are called risky.

props.name: methanol synthesis catalyst (Australian methanol plant)
props.description: The catalyst of the methanol converter; the source names it only as 'a catalyst' and gives no composition, preparation or reduction.

evidence.quote: Methanol is synthesised by passing a mixture of gases consisting of two part of hydrogen to one of CO over a catalyst at 350 - 360 ats and 350 - 400 °C.

props.name: austenitic steel against hydrogen attack
props.statement: 18/8 austenitic stainless steel is used in those parts of the ammonia and methanol converters subject to high temperature, for its resistance to hydrogen attack.

props.name: conversion up to 2 percent

evidence.quote: A conversion of up to 2% Is obtained.
The unconverted gas is recirculated by means of a booster pump.

props.statement: A conversion of up to 2% is obtained in the methanol converter; the methanol formed is condensed and contains approximately 20% water, and the unconverted gas is recirculated.

props.name: converter simpler than ammonia
props.statement: The methanol converter and circulation system are generally similar to but less elaborate than those used for ammonia synthesis; the gas passes through an interchanger with a by-pass, down through the catalyst and back through the interchanger.

props.name: crude methanol contains iron carbonyl

evidence.quote: The crude methanol from the synthesis plant contains up to 20% water and traces of iron carbonyl, ammonia, and organic compounds.

props.statement: The crude methanol from the synthesis plant contains up to 20% water and traces of iron carbonyl, ammonia and organic compounds; the iron carbonyl is removed by doping the crude spirit with 40% caustic and blowing with air for 24 hours.

props.name: feed composition set by ammonia plant
props.statement: The composition of the gas entering the methanol system is largely controlled by the requirements of the ammonia plant and the ability of the CO2 removal and CO removal plants to handle the corresponding gas rate.

props.name: interchanger failure mimics activity loss

evidence.quote: Ammonia and Methanol Synthesis Plants

props.statement: In the ammonia and methanol synthesis converters an interchanger failure is difficult to distinguish from loss of catalyst activity, since both result in reduced conversion and a lower exit-gas temperature; a gland or sheath failure causes a sudden loss of catalyst temperature.

props.name: liquid methanol cuts mild steel joints
props.statement: Liquid methanol under pressure will quickly cut the surface of a leaking mild-steel pipe joint; the pipe ends are therefore tipped with a welded deposit of hard alloy steel and stainless-steel lens rings are used for these joints.

props.name: little control of temperature gradient
props.statement: Very little control is obtainable over the temperature gradient through the methanol catalyst, and only by variation of the circulation rate; the inlet temperature of the gas going to the catalyst is controlled by adjusting the interchanger by-pass.

props.name: methanol converter failure easier to trace
props.statement: The cause of failure in a methanol converter is easier to trace than in an ammonia converter because of its simpler construction.

props.name: methanol reaction heat

props.statement: The methanol synthesis reaction may be represented as CO + 2H2 = CH3OH with 24.6 kg cal liberated.

props.name: methanol unit ancillary to ammonia
props.statement: The methanol synthesis plant is run as an ancillary unit to the ammonia synthesis plant and normally would not operate unless the ammonia plant was synthesising ammonia; gas is piped from the compressor to the methanol circulation system and bled back to the inlet of the CO removal plant.

props.name: refined methanol specification

evidence.quote: (3) Methanol - greater than 99%

props.statement: With careful control of the continuous distillation it is possible to produce refined methanol meeting the stated specification, including methanol greater than 99%.

props.name: shift equilibrium versus rate
props.statement: As the iron-steam (shift) reaction is an exothermic equilibrium reaction, lower temperatures favour hydrogen production but reduce the reaction velocity considerably; to balance these, two catalyst beds of three trays with an intermediate interchanger are used.

props.name: synthesis pressure 350 ats
props.statement: The synthesis pressure of 350 ats on the Australian plants strikes an economic balance between the costs of compression, the size of plant and the conversion efficiencies obtained.

props.name: water scrubbing removes sulphur

evidence.quote: In the CO2 removal plant the major portion of the CO2 is removed by counter current scrubbing with water under pressure.
This water scrubbing under pressure is also beneficial as it removes organic sulphur compounds and some of the traces of H28 which are still present in the gas.

props.statement: Countercurrent water scrubbing under pressure (125 lb/sq in gauge) removes the major portion of the CO2 and also removes organic sulphur compounds and some of the traces of H2S still in the gas.

props.note: the coil water pressure is 50 kg/cm2 in this plant versus 300 kg/cm2 in the former Fauser type; the purpose is the author's surmise ('思われる')
props.statement: The Fauser process removes reaction heat by natural circulation of water in cooling coils separate from the gas circuit and recovers it as steam, whereas other processes control temperature by the recycle gas rate or cold-gas injection between beds; in this plant the coil water is at 50 kg/cm2 instead of the 300 kg/cm2 of the former Fauser type, which seems to aim at a larger cooling capacity and easier circulation, with a simpler coil system.

props.name: methane formation above 400 °C causes runaway

props.name: Montecatini new Fauser methanol converter, Oyubari plant
props.description: Electric heater at the top (start-up only); four catalyst baskets with a cooling coil at the outlet of each; below them one multitubular catalyst bed and at the bottom a multitubular heat exchanger. Feed enters at the bottom exchanger, is preheated, cools the multitubular bed through the tube walls, rises along the converter wall and enters the first bed from the top. Reaction heat is removed by natural circulation of water in the coils (50 kg/cm2 instead of 300 kg/cm2 in the former Fauser type); the steam heats a recovery boiler (10 kg/cm2) at the top; each coil has a control valve for the bed temperature.

props.statement: The crude methanol was assumed, in rough agreement with industrial data, to contain besides methanol dimethyl ether, isobutyl alcohol, a di-isopropyl alcohol and oil (heptene); dimethyl ether is removed by a pre-distillation.

props.name: design conversion 15 % per pass

evidence.quote: Bij een conversie van 15 % (betrokken op CO-invoer) ligt (voor de verdere hierna gekozen reactie-condities) wel het economisch optimum.

props.statement: A conversion of 15 % per pass (on CO fed) is the economic optimum: a very high conversion needs so long a contact time that too many by-products form and the reactor becomes too large; a very low conversion gives too large a circulation and pumping cost and a harder separation of crude methanol.

props.name: design H2/CO 3.7 at converter inlet
props.statement: The H2/CO ratio in the converter inlet gas was set at 3.7; in practice 3.5 to 4 is used.

props.name: design pressure 260 atm
props.statement: The working pressure was set at 260 atm, a compromise between the more favourable equilibrium at higher pressure and the larger equipment and compression costs.

props.name: design reaction temperature about 330 °C
props.statement: The reaction temperature of the converter is about 330 °C: at lower temperature the reaction rate is too low; much higher, the equilibrium shifts unfavourably and more by-products form.

props.name: equilibrium constants newton dodge

props.statement: The gas load of a methanol reactor working under analogous conditions and with the same catalyst is about 40,000 Nm3/hr per m3 of catalyst; for the 38,830 Nm3/hr of this reactor a catalyst volume of 1 m3 was taken.

props.name: heat of methanol formation
props.note: 21600 is printed with the unit kcal/mol, 21,6 kcal on p. 5
props.statement: The heat released in methanol formation is 21600 kcal/mol (as printed); the methanol production is 43.9 kmol per hour, giving a heat release of 950,000 kcal/hr in the reactor.

props.name: high pressure favours conversion
props.statement: Because of the volume decrease of the reaction, high pressure (a few hundred atm) favours the conversion considerably.

props.name: inert gas 13 percent
props.statement: There is an optimum inert-gas (mainly N2) percentage in the recycle gas: a high percentage gives high pumping costs and a less favourable conversion, a low one needs much purge; in practice it is allowed to rise to about 13 %.

props.name: narrow temperature window
props.statement: The temperature range in which the synthesis can be realized is small: well below 300 °C the reaction rate is so small that the reactor capacity becomes very low; above 400 °C the equilibrium becomes unfavourable.

props.name: nh3 o2 injection sulfur
props.statement: Beforehand the gas is injected with 0.5 g NH3 per m3 gas with some O2 to oxidize the sulfur compounds.

props.name: no temperature gradient needed

evidence.quote: Het bl,ijkt dan (zie bijlage 4), dat de evenwichtsbena- , dering bij 340°0 en 360°0 resp. 22,8 % en 26,6 % is.

props.statement: Since equilibrium is far from being approached at both 340 °C and 360 °C (equilibrium approach 22.8 % and 26.6 %), applying an optimal falling temperature gradient over the reactor has no point.

props.name: recycle ratio 9 74
props.statement: The material balance gives a recycle ratio (reactor gas B / fresh feed A, in moles) of x = 9.74.

props.name: design choice: methanol from CO and H2
props.statement: Method A, high-pressure synthesis from CO and H2, was chosen because by-products were not wanted and the aim was only methanol with the lowest possible hydrogen consumption.

props.name: small co2 excess not removed
props.statement: The small excess of CO2 in the synthesis gas does not disturb the methanol synthesis and can also be converted to methanol, so removing it was not considered worthwhile; the amount is too small to justify a CO2 absorption plant.

props.name: zno absorbs sulfur
props.statement: Although the natural gas was assumed sulfur-free, the gas can if needed be passed through a tank of cylindrical zinc-oxide tablets (0.1875 x 0.5 in.) that convert H2S and mercaptans into ZnS.

evidence.locator: p. 7, D. Keuze van het proces

props.statement: The CO conversion is in general the best process for methanol; hydrogen consumption and the purity of the crude methanol were decisive in this choice.

props.name: co2 process disadvantages
props.statement: The CO2 hydrogenation process is run under practically the same conditions as the CO process; its disadvantages are the purity of the crude methanol (by-products dimethyl ether, isopropyl alcohol, isobutyl alcohol, higher alcohols and esters; at most 75 % methanol) and a hydrogen consumption per methanol 1.5 times that of the CO process. It was first applied in the US by the Commercial Solvents Corporation (lit. 2).

props.name: industrial conditions
props.note: cited from lit. 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7
props.statement: In industry pressures of 250 to 350 atm, temperatures of 300 to 375 °C and space velocities of 30,000-50,000 are used (lit. 1, 3, 5, 6); very pure crude methanol (95-99 %) is obtained; with these high space velocities the CO conversion per pass is only about 12-16 % (lit. 2, 3, 7), far from equilibrium.

props.name: methanation most harmful
props.statement: Methane formation (CO + 3 H2 -> CH4 + H2O) is the most harmful side reaction: it is very strongly exothermic, more so than methanol formation, and can lead to hot spots; hot spots and the associated ruin of the catalyst must be prevented.

props.name: natta adsorbed phase h2 co ratio

evidence.note: read as 'a larger yield is obtained when in the synthesis gas c(H2)/c(CO) > 2'; quote withheld: sha256:3431244d6cd4477ab70195fb4f725b850257373e4964615ea75ba05182b31b39 chars:129

props.note: cited from Natta, 'Catalysis' vol. 3 (Emmett, ed., 1955) (lit. 3)
props.statement: With very selective catalysts a larger yield is obtained when the H2/CO ratio in the synthesis gas exceeds 2. Natta showed that the CO-H2 reaction is described quite well by a mechanism in the adsorbed phase, and that at large space velocities CO is adsorbed much faster than H2; so an H2/CO ratio above two must be applied in the gas to obtain the stoichiometric ratio of two in the adsorbed phase.

props.name: no iron nickel

evidence.note: '~zer' = ijzer (iron); '4000C' read as 400 °C; quote withheld: sha256:96ed2b43f5840a4edaa1a9db2db89550f8f84395080f58c14ee7589476525fe2 chars:134

props.statement: The catalyst must contain no iron or nickel, which catalyze the conversion of CO to CH4, especially above 400 °C; at lower temperatures (about 370 °C) even traces are not ruinous. Very active iron or nickel can deposit on the catalyst by decomposition of Fe(CO)5 or Ni(CO)4, which must therefore not be present in the synthesis gas.

props.name: oil lowers activity
props.statement: Oil droplets are always carried along by the gas when it is compressed; the oil is adsorbed on the catalyst and strongly lowers its activity, so it must be removed from the synthesis gas.

props.name: pressure and inerts
props.statement: CO + 2 H2 -> CH3OH proceeds with a large decrease in volume, so raising the total pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right; with inert gases such as N2 in the synthesis gas even higher pressures are needed, since the rate depends on the activities (proportional to the partial pressures) of CO and H2.

props.name: purge constant composition

evidence.locator: p. 13, III Beschrijving van de procesgang
evidence.quote: Een deel van het circulatiegas wordt gespuid om te bewerks t ellige~,dat de samenstelling van het gas, dat naar de re actor gaat, steeds constant zal z ~n.

props.statement: Part of the circulating gas is purged so that the composition of the gas to the reactor stays constant; otherwise the inert gases (N2, CH4) would accumulate and lower the yield.

props.name: selective catalyst needed
props.statement: Of the many possible reactions of CO and H2 the equilibrium of CO + 2 H2 -> CH3OH is the least favourable, so a very selective and active catalyst is needed and the usual hydrogenation catalysts cannot be used; the reaction is feasible only over a limited temperature range: below 300 °C the rate is too small and above 400 °C the equilibrium is very unfavourable.

props.name: selective catalysts found
props.note: cited from lit. 3 (Natta) and 5 (Groggins)
props.statement: It has proved possible (lit. 3, 5) to find catalysts that promote exclusively the reduction of CO to methanol while all other side reactions are almost completely suppressed, at least when the temperature does not exceed 390 °C.

props.name: stainless steel against co

evidence.quote: Doordat soms plaatsel~k heel hoge tempe- raturen voorkomen,kan de bekleding smelten.Het is daarom in moderne fabrieken gebruikel~k om de reactor,de W.W.,de condensor,de productafscheider en de p~pen van Doestvr~ staal (18 Cr- 8Ni staalV te maken.

props.statement: CO can react with the walls of the reactor, heat exchanger, condenser and pipes, and the iron carbonyl formed is very harmful to the activity of the catalyst; a thin copper or bronze lining is not always sufficient because it can melt at local very high temperatures, so modern plants make these of stainless steel (18 Cr-8 Ni).

props.name: synthesis gas raw materials

evidence.locator: p. 9, F. plaats van de fabriek

props.statement: CO and H2 can be made in many ways; the most important raw materials are water gas (steam over glowing coke at 1000 °C, or methane/natural gas with steam at 800 °C over a nickel catalyst; higher hydrocarbons and refinery off-gases can also be used), thermal cracking of hydrocarbons (hydrogen as a by-product of carbon-black manufacture) and CO as a by-product of calcium-carbide manufacture; the plant is best placed near ample coke or natural gas.

props.statement: The results confirm Garner's suggestion that the irreversible adsorption of carbon monoxide takes place on an acceptor site.

props.name: CO acts as an electron donor in the adsorption: raising the Fermi level with Ga2
props.statement: CO acts as an electron donor in the adsorption: raising the Fermi level with Ga2O3 decreased the heat of adsorption, and lowering it with Li2O so facilitated electron donation that reduction became too rapid to measure the adsorption.

props.name: Owing to the reduction effect the higher pressure sections of the CO isotherms a
props.statement: Owing to the reduction effect the higher pressure sections of the CO isotherms are of doubtful value, and the isosteric heats may be considerably in error at higher coverages.

props.name: The CO2 isotherms on all three adsorbents are typically chemisorption isotherms;
props.statement: The CO2 isotherms on all three adsorbents are typically chemisorption isotherms; chemisorption is confirmed by isosteric heats of 16-28 Kcal per mole.

props.name: The maximum CO2 adsorption measured (about 5 x 10-6 moles/m2) corresponds to a s
props.statement: The maximum CO2 adsorption measured (about 5 x 10-6 moles/m2) corresponds to a surface coverage of about one half, assuming an effective cross section of about 16 A2 for CO2 and SO2.

props.name: CO2 acts as an electron acceptor in the adsorption: Ga2O3, which increases elect
props.statement: CO2 acts as an electron acceptor in the adsorption: Ga2O3, which increases electron availability in ZnO, increases the heat of adsorption, and Li2O, which depresses the Fermi level, decreases it; a high electron concentration in the adsorbent increases the strength of the adsorption bond.

props.name: Plotted against surface coverage (moles/m2), the CO2 heats of adsorption on the
props.statement: Plotted against surface coverage (moles/m2), the CO2 heats of adsorption on the three adsorbents diverge as coverage decreases: very marked differences at low coverage, barely any at high coverage.

props.name: The hydrogen heats of adsorption are in an unexpected order for the three adsorb
props.statement: The hydrogen heats of adsorption are in an unexpected order for the three adsorbents and appear to increase with coverage; whether this is significant or due to erroneous readings caused by reduction cannot be said with any certainty.

props.name: Hydrogen also reduced the zinc oxide at the temperatures used: the zinc deposit
props.statement: Hydrogen also reduced the zinc oxide at the temperatures used: the zinc deposit in the adsorption tube and the darkening of the pellets are strong evidence for reduction and help refute intra-lattice adsorption; the hydrogen isotherms were most unsatisfactory because of reduction effects.

props.name: CO2 isotherms obey the Langmuir equation reasonably well only above about 0.3 mm
props.statement: CO2 isotherms obey the Langmuir equation reasonably well only above about 0.3 mm Hg; the Freundlich equation holds for CO2 on ZnO and on ZnO + Ga2O3 from 10-2 to 1 mm Hg but not on ZnO + Li2O; CO isotherms obey Langmuir fairly well above about 0.3 mm Hg and never obey Freundlich.

props.name: For the adsorbent with the lowest Fermi level, ZnO + 0.5 mole % Li2O, the reduct
props.statement: For the adsorbent with the lowest Fermi level, ZnO + 0.5 mole % Li2O, the reduction effect of CO was most marked, so that equilibrium pressures could not be measured even for the smaller adsorptions.

props.name: Although the adsorbents were prepared by as closely similar methods as possible,
props.statement: Although the adsorbents were prepared by as closely similar methods as possible, addition of 0.5 mole % Ga2O3 almost doubled the surface area of the zinc oxide and 0.5 mole % Li2O increased it; the reason is at present obscure.

props.name: Because of thermomolecular flow the heats of adsorption are a little below their
props.statement: Because of thermomolecular flow the heats of adsorption are a little below their true values; a 4% error is the largest possible (recalculation for H2 on ZnO + Ga2O3 at 1.5 x 10-6 moles/gm showed 14.2 Kcal per mole to be only 4% too low); relative values between the three adsorbents are correct.

props.name: The Fermi level in the adsorbent is of primary importance in determining the hea
props.statement: The Fermi level in the adsorbent is of primary importance in determining the heat of CO2 adsorption only at low coverage; at higher coverage other factors such as repulsive interactions between molecules become more important.

props.name: In the reduction by hydrogen water would be formed and most probably rapidly ads
props.statement: In the reduction by hydrogen water would be formed and most probably rapidly adsorbed.

props.name: The rapid extra adsorption of hydrogen on lowering the temperature (Frankenburg'
props.statement: The rapid extra adsorption of hydrogen on lowering the temperature (Frankenburg's method) is explained by two types of adsorption sites, one with negligible and one with considerable activation energy of adsorption; either the new state is true equilibrium, or equilibrium on the high activation energy sites is frozen in, so that only the highest temperature isotherm represents true equilibrium.

props.name: Reduction of the zinc oxide by carbon monoxide was taking place: above a certain
props.statement: Reduction of the zinc oxide by carbon monoxide was taking place: above a certain CO pressure the reaction rate becomes measurable, the CO2 produced is immediately adsorbed (causing the continued pressure drop), and the zinc formed darkens the adsorbent and sublimes to the cooler parts of the apparatus (the deposit).

props.method: precipitation of nickel hydroxide from a hot ~1% nickel nitrate solution with ammonium hydroxide; settling, decanting, centrifuging, washing, drying in 1 cm layers, breaking into granules
steps: a solution of nickel nitrate Ni(NO3)2.6H2O or similar soluble nickel salt is made up in distilled water to a concentration of about 1%
the solution is heated to 95-100° C. and treated with sufficient ammonium hydroxide to just render it alkaline, as indicated by 'brilliant yellow' indicator paper
the precipitate is allowed to settle and the supernatant liquor removed by siphoning or decantation
the precipitated nickel hydroxide is separated, e.g. by centrifuging, washed with about five times its volume of distilled water and separated again with a centrifuge
the moist precipitate is spread out on plates in layers about 1 cm in thickness and dried at 100-105° C. for about 10-15 hours
the hard dense cakes are broken up into granules of a size suitable for catalytic use

props.statement: A process for unsaturated hydrocarbons and methanol: (1) react a feedstock of hydrocarbons, hydrogen and oxygen above 1200 °C to a product containing acetylene, ethylene, methane, hydrogen, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide (printed: hydrocarbon:carbon monoxide volume ratio greater than 1:1); (2) remove successively carbon dioxide, acetylene and ethylene, leaving methane, hydrogen and carbon monoxide with hydrogen:carbon monoxide volume ratio greater than 1:1; (3) convert catalytically a substantial amount of hydrogen and carbon monoxide to methanol in a methanol converter; (4) condense the methanol and scrub the unreacted gases under elevated pressure with recycled product methanol, forming a solution of methane in methanol; (5) remove the solution, decrease its pressure and liberate the methane; (6) recycle product methanol to step (4); (7) recycle the scrubbed gases to the converter.

graph.description: Cutoff: published or publicly disclosed before 1966-01-01. ICI launched low-pressure methanol synthesis over Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 in 1966 (GB 1,010,871, published 1966; US 3,326,956); a cutoff of 1 January 1966 holds out that commercialization and what followed as rediscovery targets, and admits everything published before it, ICI's earlier publications included. The cutoff does not remove every Cu-Zn-Al disclosure: the corpus leakage audit (historical/LEAKAGE_AUDIT.md) lists US 2,061,470 (Larson, granted 1936), whose Example 10 is 87 CuO / 10 ZnO / 3 Al2O3, and Cu-Zn catalysts from 1928 on. They are in scope and curated as reported; a rediscovery evaluation must hold them out separately if it needs to. Each source was read and curated from its page texts (PDF text layer, or Tesseract OCR where the PDF has none); every quote is checked verbatim against those texts. Earlier extractions were used only as checklists. Scoped to CO and CO2 hydrogenation to methanol: tests of other reactions, the records only they use and the claims resting only on them are left out (tools/curation.py scope_methanol_synthesis).
